# Chapter 5 — Theories

By the following Friday the speaking had happened six times that anyone was counting, and people were counting.

Priya had put a whiteboard up in the station, which was a thing she had resisted for two years on the grounds that whiteboards invited bad thinking. She wrote on it now in her small, tidy handwriting: *Event 1 — Nov 12 — Global, coastal, ~90s. Event 2 — Nov 14 — Pacific basin only, ~40s. Event 3* — and so on. The last column she had labeled *affect* and in that column she had written things like *grief-adj.* and *unclassed* and, for event four, just a question mark.

"I don't like the question mark," Maren said.

"Neither do I."

"It's doing something."

"It's doing the only honest thing on that board."

Priya had a theory. She had it by the end of that week and she was working it hard. The structures, she thought, were acting as resonance chambers — not transmitting, not speaking, but *amplifying* something that had been in the water already, below the threshold of what hydrophones could pick up. The die-offs and the speaking were correlated because the speaking required the dying. The dying animal was the terminal point of whatever the signal was doing. She'd started calling it *terminal vocalization* in her notes and then crossed it out because she said she didn't want to name it after anything.

Maren had a different theory. She thought the patterns in the signal looked like compressed cetacean social communication — that what they were hearing was whalesong that had been, somehow, condensed in time and released at the moment of death in other species. She did not believe this very hard. She believed it enough to say it out loud to Priya twice and then to stop saying it because Priya's face did a thing.

Neither of them believed their own theory by Monday. They kept them up anyway because it was easier to work against a theory than to work in nothing.

The week got away from her. She missed a 2 p.m. call with Corvallis and Priya took it and did not mention it. She forgot to call her father back on Tuesday and remembered on Wednesday and decided she would call Thursday and didn't. She went to the Coast Guard station bar on Wednesday night, which was called the Sou'wester and which she had been avoiding for eight months, and sat at the end of the bar and drank three beers and ended up in the parking lot with a petty officer named Kyle who was maybe thirty-one and who had a kind face and a wife in San Diego, which he mentioned, and which she heard, and which did not change what they did.

She drove home at one in the morning. The road along the bay was empty. She was not drunk enough to be in trouble and not sober enough to feel good about driving, and she kept the window down and the radio off and thought, with a kind of clinical interest, that she had not done anything like that in sixteen years and had just done it, and that she felt approximately how she'd expected to feel, which was not very much. She filed it. She was good at filing.

Thursday morning she went into the station with a headache and Priya did not say anything about her face and they worked. They had a backlog. A fisheries technician from the Quinault Nation had sent over tissue samples and a note that said *we are seeing this too, please advise if you learn anything*. Maren read the note four times. *Please advise if you learn anything.* She did not know what she would write back.

At noon Priya came in with her laptop and put it on the desk between them and said, "Watch this."

It was phone footage from a beach in Peru. Maren could tell it was Peru because there were words at the bottom of the frame in Spanish that she couldn't read. It was event four. A woman was filming her own feet at first and then lifted the phone and panned it, shakily, across a long line of dying fish — a species Maren didn't immediately know, something silver and slender — and in the shot you could see, clearly, their mouths moving. The camera caught the audio. Not well. The phone's microphone was not built for this. But there was a pattern audible under the woman's breathing.

"Listen to the pattern," Priya said, and paused it and rewound and played again. "Listen."

Three short. One long. Three short. One long. Then a fifth thing, a rising, and then a flat.

Maren watched it through twice. She said, "Yeah, that's what we have."

"That's what we have."

"Okay."

"From Peru."

"Yeah."

"Same phrase. Exact same. I ran it against event three's hydrophone, the Astoria file. It lines up to within about forty milliseconds."

"Across what distance."

"Eight thousand miles."

"Okay."

Priya looked at her.

"Maren."

"I heard you."

"I'm going to send this to Scripps."

"Send it."

Priya went back to her desk. Maren sat with the laptop open in front of her and watched the clip four more times. The three-short one-long, she had felt in her sternum on the bay road nine days ago, coming through the concrete of the gas station, coming out of the mouth of a rockfish on a beach half a mile from her house.

She had felt the same phrase. At the same time. That a woman in Peru was filming with shaking hands.

She did not tell Priya about the rockfish. She did not tell Priya about the bay road. She did not know why she wasn't telling her and she chose, specifically, not to examine this. She closed the laptop and slid it back across the desk. She said she was going to take a walk.

She walked to the end of the gravel lot and stood there for ten minutes and came back in and did not say anything more about Peru.

# Chapter 6 — Jorgen

*Go see your dad*, Priya texted Saturday morning. *I'll cover your 2pm. Don't make this a thing.*

Maren stared at the text for a long time. Priya's messages always had the effect of being slightly in charge of her, which she resented, and obeyed.

She stopped at the Safeway on the way over and bought a rotisserie chicken and a bag of those rolls he liked and a six-pack of the Rainier he drank and she did not drink. The cashier was a kid she did not recognize, which happened now. When she was growing up she had known every cashier at the Safeway.

Jorgen had the TV on when she came in. Of course he did. He had it on the news and the news was running the Peru footage, the one Priya had showed her, over and over in a loop with a chyron underneath that said *COORDINATED EVENT — ANALYSIS ONGOING*. He was sitting in his chair with his coffee on the side table going cold and he did not get up when she came in.

"Hey, Dad."

"Hey, Mare." He didn't look away from the TV. "You see this one?"

"Yeah."

"They keep playing it."

"I see that."

"It's the same one. They've been playing the same one since Tuesday."

She put the bag on the kitchen counter. She called from the kitchen, "You want me to heat this up?"

"Sure."

She heated it. He did not come into the kitchen. When she brought his plate in he took it without looking at her and set it on his lap and she sat down on the couch with her own plate and they ate like that, facing the TV, which was what they had been doing on and off for thirty-five years. The footage looped. The woman's feet. The silver fish. The pan up the beach.

"I think it's from God," he said, around a mouthful of chicken.

"Dad."

"I'm just saying what I think."

"It's not from God."

"Well, you don't know."

"I know it's not from God."

"How."

"Because it's not, Dad. Because that's — that's not what this is."

"What is it then."

"I don't know."

"Okay. So."

"So because I don't know doesn't mean it's from God."

"No, but it doesn't mean it isn't."

"Dad."

"Mare, I'm seventy-one years old, I'm allowed to think what I think."

"Fine."

"I'm just saying."

"Fine."

They ate. On the TV the clip cut to a panel of experts. Jorgen made a small dismissive sound at one of them, a woman with glasses, and Maren did not ask why.

After a while he said, "You hear from your mother?"

"No."

"She said she was gonna call you."

"She didn't."

"Huh." He chewed. "Well."

"Dad."

"I'm just saying *huh*."

"You're not just saying *huh*."

He looked at her for the first time since she'd come in. "Mare. Come on."

"What."

"I'm not — I'm not doing anything."

"You do this."

"What do I do."

"You do this — this — *well-huh* thing and it's always about her and it's always like I'm supposed to do something about it."

"I didn't say you were supposed to do anything."

"You never do. That's the whole thing. You just — you just leave it there."

"Mare."

"What."

He set his plate down on the side table. He said, carefully, in the voice he used when he thought he was being reasonable:

"Well, maybe if you'd tried a little harder with him."

"What."

"With Daniel. I'm just saying. I liked him. He called me, you know. After. He called to tell me."

"He called *you*."

"He did. He was — he was upset."

"He called you and you didn't tell me."

"What was I going to tell you. You'd already done it."

"Jesus Christ, Dad."

"I liked him."

"You liked him because he called you on your birthday."

"That's not a small thing, Mare."

"I'm going."

"Mare."

"I'm going."

She got up. She got her coat. He did not get up. She stood in the hallway with her coat half on and said, to the wall, not to him, "You don't get to do this today."

"Do what."

"This."

She left.

She got in the truck and drove. She got to the highway and turned left toward home and got about four miles and pulled into the turnout at the Chinook overlook and sat there with the truck running and her hands on the wheel and did not cry, because she did not cry, and then she put the truck in reverse and turned around and drove back.

He was on the porch when she pulled in. He had his coat on. He was holding a garbage bag.

"There's a heron in the yard," he said, as if she had just been out to the store. "I was gonna get it."

"I'll get it."

"Mare."

"I'll get it, Dad."

She got it. It was a big one, wet, its neck folded wrong. She put it in the bag and tied the bag and walked it to the can at the side of the house. When she came back he was sitting on the porch step. She sat down next to him. They did not talk. The porch light was on even though it was still light out. The Subaru had a little skim of rain on it. After a while he said, "It's cold out here," and she said, "Yeah," and neither of them got up.

She drove home at dusk. On the bay road it came again — three short, one long, the longer fifth thing after — and she pulled the truck onto the shoulder and got out and stood in the grass by the ditch with her hands in her jacket pockets and listened.

It went on for a while this time. In the middle of it there was a stretch that was flat and slow and, she realized later, boring — a long unshaped passage where nothing happened, where the pressure just *continued*, not grieving, not anything, just going, like a sentence that did not end because whoever was saying it did not need it to.

That was the part that stayed with her.

# Chapter 7 — What It Is Not

Priya called at four in the morning.

"Get up."

"I'm up."

"You weren't up."

"I'm up now."

"There's going to be a big one. NOAA's calling it. The Sounder's out and they're seeing the precursors — whatever the precursors are — and they think it's in the next two hours. Get dressed. I'll pick you up."

"Where are we going."

"The beach. Where else."

Priya picked her up in the blue Subaru with two thermoses of coffee in the cup holders and her hair still wet from the shower. They did not talk on the drive. The road was empty. It was not yet light. When they came over the rise at the beach access the ocean was that pre-dawn grey that was almost no color, and the structure on the horizon was doing its thing to the sky above it, which you could see better in low light, a kind of dimness that held its shape.

There were more people on the beach than Maren expected. Twenty, thirty. Some of them were locals she knew by face. Some were not. A family had set up on a blanket like it was the Fourth of July, the mother with a thermos, two kids half-asleep against her. A teenager was filming already, phone held up, nothing yet to film. An older man, maybe seventy, in a long coat, was walking the tideline alone and slowly with his hands behind his back.

Priya parked. They walked down to the sand. The tide was out and the line of dying fish was already there — a broader line than Maren had seen yet, varied, sand lance and smelt and a small run of jack mackerel she didn't understand the presence of. The gulls were not on them. That was the thing she noticed first. The gulls were standing twenty yards back in a loose cluster, not eating, not moving.

"Yeah," Priya said, looking at the gulls. "Okay."

They waited. It got light, slowly. The family on the blanket opened a tupperware of something. The teenager lowered his phone and then raised it again. The older man kept walking his line. Nobody was talking much. A couple Maren didn't know were standing close together near the dune grass and the woman was holding the man's arm with both hands.

It started at about six fifteen.

It started the way the last one had started, through the ground first, three and one, soft, the kind of soft that was not really soft but was the body adjusting to hearing something it had not yet registered. Then it came up. It came up the way a tide comes up. She had time to notice this — time to notice that she had time — and then it was there.

The fish along the line moved their mouths. All of them, at once, the same shape, opening and closing in the pattern. The pattern was long this time. The three-and-one went and went and then it changed. The fifth thing came in, the rising. Then the flat stretch, the long flat, the thing from the bay road that she had thought was boring and that, now, on the open beach, with thirty people standing in it, was not boring at all. It was something else. She did not have the word.

Priya made a sound next to her. Not a word. A sound.

And then the other things came. The things that were not grief or recognition or satiation. A color-sensation pushed into her chest that she could only describe, later, as *downward red* — a red that was going away from her, into the sand, through the sand — and under that a feeling like *being counted*, a specific, clerical, almost bureaucratic feeling, like being a line item on something long, and under that a feeling she had no name for at all, a feeling that seemed to be the feeling *of* a large quantity of small things at once, not grief for them, not about them, just *of* them, as if she were being briefly made into that quantity and then released.

The family on the blanket — the mother had her hand over her mouth. One of the kids was asleep through it. The other kid was staring. The teenager had lowered his phone and was not filming. The couple by the dune grass had separated. The older man had stopped walking and was standing in the wet sand with his coat hem in the water and was not moving. As she watched he took three steps into the water, up to his knees, and stood there. He did not look upset. He looked like someone who had remembered something.

It went on. It went on longer than any of them had gone on. Five minutes. Seven. A part of her was counting. A part of her was not anywhere.

And in the middle of it she understood, without language for the understanding, that it was not for her. Not for them. Not for the thirty people on the beach and not for the species and not for the planet in any sense that she had been using that word. It was happening in their presence. They were near it. They were not its reason. The grief in it was not human grief and the recognition in it was not recognizing them and the counting in it was not counting them. They were overhearing. They had been overhearing the whole time.

It ended. It ended in the middle of a phrase, it seemed to her, though she could not have said why.

Priya was crying. She was bent a little at the waist with her hands on her knees like someone who had just finished running. She said, "I'm sorry. I'm — sorry. I don't know why I'm apologizing. Jesus. Give me a second."

Maren put her hand on Priya's back. It was the first time she had touched Priya on purpose in two years of working with her. She left it there until Priya straightened up.

The old man came out of the water. He walked past them up the beach without looking at anyone and got into a green truck and drove away.

In the Subaru on the way back Maren tried to call her father. He didn't pick up.

She did not tell Priya what she had understood. She did not know how, and she did not, in any case, find it comforting. She found it lonely in a way she had not been lonely before, which was a new and specific loneliness, and she sat with it in the passenger seat with her hands flat on her thighs and watched the highway and did not speak.

# Chapter 8 — After

She went to Jorgen's on Sunday. He had picked up, eventually, Saturday night, and said he'd been in the shower, which she didn't believe and didn't challenge. He'd sounded tired. He'd asked if she was coming over and she'd said yes without thinking about it, which was new.

She stopped at the Safeway again. She bought eggs, bacon, the kind of bread he liked, a carton of orange juice because he'd mentioned once that he liked orange juice and she had filed it. The cashier today was a woman she had gone to high school with whose name she could not retrieve. The woman said, "Hey, Maren," and Maren said, "Hey," and the woman bagged the groceries and neither of them said anything else.

He was on the porch when she pulled in. He had his coat on over his pajamas and his slippers on and a coffee.

"You'll freeze," she said.

"I'm fine."

"You're in your slippers."

"I'm on the porch, Mare, I'm not going anywhere."

She made breakfast. He sat at the kitchen table and watched her do it, which he had never done in her life, and which she decided not to comment on. The TV was off for once. That was also new. She scrambled the eggs the way he liked them, which was overcooked, and fried the bacon crisp, and put it all on a plate with two slices of the bread toasted and buttered and set it in front of him. She made herself the same.

"Eggs are dry," he said.

"That's how you like them."

"They're drier than that."

"Eat them, Dad."

He ate them. He ate all of them. He drank the orange juice and made a face at it because it was the pulpy kind and he did not like pulp and she had forgotten, or had not known, or had known and forgotten, and she did not apologize. He drank it anyway.

They moved to the living room after. He put the TV on. There was a Mariners game from the archives, a rerun, 2001, which he had watched probably a hundred times, which he put on now at low volume and did not really watch. She sat on the couch. He sat in his chair. Outside, it was not raining, which was rare for the time of year. The light came in the front window in a thin flat way.

"You hear the one last week," he said, at some point.

"Yeah."

"On the beach."

"Yeah."

"I didn't go down."

"I know."

"Gary went down. He said it was — he said he didn't know."

"Yeah."

"He cried, he said."

"A lot of people cried."

"Did you."

"No."

"Huh." He watched the TV for a minute. Ichiro was at the plate. "Your mother called again."

She did not say anything.

"I told her you were busy."

"Okay."

"She said — she said she might come out. In the spring."

"Okay."

"I told her I'd tell you."

"Okay."

He did not say anything more about it. She did not either. Ichiro hit a single and Jorgen grunted a small approving sound and drank his coffee. She thought, for a second, about saying the thing — the thing from when she was sixteen, the thing she had never said to anyone — and she opened her mouth a little and then closed it. The moment came and went the way a wave comes and goes, and she let it, and she was not, she realized, going to say it today, and probably not ever, and something in her that had been braced for twenty-three years was, briefly and not completely, not braced.

She noticed he had gotten smaller. She had been noticing this for months without letting it be a thing she had noticed, and she let it be, now, a thing she had noticed. He was smaller in the chair than he had been a year ago. His hands on the armrests were the hands of an old man, which she had not let them be before.

"Yeah."

"No."

"Okay."

There had been no speaking that day that she had heard of, though she had stopped checking her phone constantly and so she would not have known.

The tap made a small sound as she shut it off, a hitch in the pipes, a thing it had done since she'd moved in, and for a second she thought it was starting again and then it wasn't. It was the pipes. [Analysis]

This chapter is a remarkably controlled piece of writing that executes its plan with considerable skill. Let me work through it systematically.

**Craft and Voice**

The prose is disciplined in exactly the way the plan demands. Short sentences do structural work without becoming a tic. The dialogue is stripped to the bone — the exchange about the hydrophone file ("Stopped why." / "Asked." / "Asked.") is genuinely good, using repetition to convey the weight of what's being communicated without explaining it. The rhythm of the Priya-outside scene, where Maren watches her through the window and Priya "did not do anything in particular, just stood in the gravel with her arms folded and looked at the tree line," is precise and earned. The restraint here is real restraint, not the performance of restraint.

The description of the hydrophone recording is handled well: "It had a period. It had a shape. Three short pulses and a longer one, and then a quality she could not describe, a kind of weight in the middle register that moved." This is specific without being falsely precise, and the "weight in the middle register that moved" is a genuinely strange formulation that earns its strangeness. The phone-call-through-a-wall simile is the chapter's most explicit metaphor and it lands cleanly — it does thematic work (overhearing, not being addressed) without announcing itself.

**The Speaking**

The rendering of the speaking is the chapter's central challenge and it largely succeeds. The three-and-one pattern is established through the hydrophone recording, then confirmed in the rockfish's mouth, then felt through the gas station concrete — a tripling that builds without becoming mechanical. The somatic quality is rendered correctly: felt in the sternum, in the feet, not heard as a voice. The gas station scene is the chapter's best passage. The woman crying silently with her eyes open, the man laughing "a real laugh, the kind you do when something is actually funny" — these are the incompatible human responses the plan called for, and they're rendered without editorializing. The man's laugh is particularly good: it's not hysterical, not wrong in an obvious way, just wrong in a specific way that's more disturbing.

**Character Consistency**

Maren is consistent with her profile throughout. She doesn't tell Priya about the rockfish. She doesn't call her father. She drives to the gas station "because the truck was a reason to be somewhere" — this is exactly the kind of self-aware-but-not-quite-honest internal notation the character profile calls for. Her hands are steady when she hangs up the nozzle. She doesn't cry or laugh. The chapter ends with her sitting in the driveway for ten minutes, which is the right kind of non-resolution.

Priya is handled well in the brief space she occupies. Her going outside, the held finger, the slow removal of headphones — these are behavioral details that feel true to the profile without being over-explained. Her line "I don't know what I'm saying" / "I know" is the chapter's best dialogue exchange: two people acknowledging the limits of language without making a speech about it.

**Following the Plan**

The chapter follows its plan closely. The hydrophone data, Priya going outside, the rockfish on the beach, the gull taking the eye, the gas station event, the woman crying, the man laughing wrong, Maren driving home with both hands on the wheel — all present and executed. The plan's note that "she does not cry or laugh" is honored. The plan's note that she doesn't tell Priya is honored. The three-beat pattern is established here as planned.

**Weaknesses**

The chapter is not without problems. "She was shaking, a little, in a way that was not cold" is slightly clunky — the qualification "in a way that was not cold" is doing work the sentence doesn't quite need, and it's the kind of construction that calls attention to itself without earning the attention. The opening scene with Priya and the headphones is very good, but the transition to the beach survey is slightly abrupt — not fatally so, but the connective tissue ("She went back to the beach that afternoon because she had a survey scheduled and because she did not know what else to do") is a little on-the-nose in its self-explanation. The plan called for Maren to "have to leave the room" after listening, but the chapter has her go outside with Priya instead, which is a reasonable adjustment but slightly softens the intended isolation.

The chapter is also, by design, not a plot-heavy chapter — it's an event chapter, a chapter of experience rather than development. This is appropriate to the story's project, but it means the "compelling plot" metric will necessarily be lower; the chapter is doing something other than plot.

**Overall**

This is accomplished literary fiction writing. The restraint is genuine, the strangeness of the speaking is rendered without false comfort or false horror, and the characters behave consistently with their profiles. The chapter does what it sets out to do and does it without significant missteps.

writing_prompt.title: Midnight Blood
writing_prompt.writing_prompt:
Darkly Comic British YA Fiction
Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸

step_outputs.1:
# Brainstorming

**Tone & Voice Options:**
- First-person teenage narrator, sharp, sardonic, self-aware — think Fleabag meets Skins meets Marina Hyde. British YA darkly comic means wit under the horror, not camp.
- Present tense could work for immediacy at midnight texting culture.
- Regional voice? Manchester, Glasgow, small Welsh town, dreary commuter belt, coastal Kent. Specificity helps.
- Class commentary baked in — comprehensive vs. grammar vs. the one posh friend.

**The Three Blood Drops — What Could It Mean:**
1. Literal: Someone's period (most banal reading, could subvert)
2. Self-harm confession/threat
3. A murder — someone's done something
4. Drug code / county lines
5. A prank gone wrong
6. A group chat ritual / friendship pact
7. Period blood as a signal that a pregnancy scare is over (relief, not horror)
8. A dare / initiation
9. A horror film reference / in-joke that becomes real
10. Menstruation confession from a trans friend
11. Someone's been attacked
12. Vampire/supernatural tease that turns out mundane — or vice versa
13. A miscarriage
14. Code between friends for "he hit me again"

**Character Possibilities:**
- Protagonist: 16-17, exam-age, sixth form, sarcastic, observant, slightly peripheral in own friend group
- Best friend: the texter — more glamorous, chaotic, the protagonist orbits her
- Love interest / red herring
- The boyfriend (potential villain)
- Parents: absent, divorced, oblivious, or darkly funny in their own way
- A teacher figure
- A nemesis — mean girl or rival

**Plot Shapes:**
A) Mystery: text leads protagonist on a night journey across town to find friend, dark comedy of errors, reveals something grim (abusive boyfriend, abortion, crime)
B) Gradual reveal: story unfolds over days/weeks after, the three dots meant something awful
C) Flashback structure: we start at aftermath and wind back
D) The text is a red herring — protagonist assumes worst, it's something mundane, but investigating uncovers something else worse
E) The three drops = three girls, three separate crises on one night
F) It's a suicide note in emoji form
G) Protagonist IS the problem — sent the text themselves, unreliable narrator

**Specific Plot Ideas:**

*Plot 1: The Night Walk*
Tilly gets text from best friend Nora at 00:04. Nora doesn't answer calls. Tilly sneaks out, tries to find her — bus stops, the boyfriend's house, the party, the hospital, the canal. Each stop reveals more. Ends with Nora safe but Tilly realising she was the last to be told, that Nora had a miscarriage, or was assaulted, or was covering for her brother who'd done something.

*Plot 2: The Pact*
Three friends, three blood drops. A pact they made drunkenly about something — revenge on a teacher/boy/each other. Now one of them is activating it. Black comedy about teenage seriousness vs. real consequences.

*Plot 3: The Group Chat*
The text is in a group chat. Everyone assumes it's about someone else. Rashomon-style? No, too complex for 8k words. But: mis-sent text, wrong number, dark consequences of assumption.

*Plot 4: Vampire Bait-and-Switch*
Protagonist convinced friend has gotten into something occult. Comedy of literalism. Real answer is gritty: heroin, abusive relationship, self-harm.

*Plot 5: The Murder*
Friend has killed someone (accidentally? Her dad? Her boyfriend?). Tilly helps cover it up. Ends with Tilly realising she's now complicit / the friend planned it / Tilly was the target.

**Chapter Pacing (Plot 1 direction):**
- Ch1: The text. Tilly's room, her family context, her relationship with Nora. Decision to go out.
- Ch2: Sneaking out. First stop — maybe Nora's house, empty/weird.
- Ch3: The boyfriend Finn's flat. Confrontation, comedy, dread.
- Ch4: Party/pub. Tilly meets others, gets info, gets wasted, red herring.
- Ch5: Hospital or police station. Dark pivot.
- Ch6: Finding Nora. Reveal.
- Ch7: Fallout. Morning. Parents. Aftermath.
- Ch8: Later. Consequences. Something unsettling — maybe Tilly realises her own role, or the friendship is over, or a final twist.

**British YA texture notes:**
- Corner shops, night buses, bus passes, Greggs, vape smoke, uni applications, UCAS stress, predictive text, Tesco meal deals, council estates vs. new-builds, Labradors, Wetherspoons, A-levels, offer letters, dad's new girlfriend, mum's wine habit, the group chat name ("Slags"), safety pins, eyeliner wings, fake IDs.
- Specific humour: understatement, deflection via joke, class anxiety, weather as character.

**Possible Endings:**
- Nora is pregnant / had miscarriage, boyfriend is awful, Tilly realises the friendship was always one-sided
- Nora has killed boyfriend (self-defence), Tilly helps
- Nora is fine, it was a joke/misunderstanding — but Tilly's night reveals her own darkness
- Nora is dead by end — suicide — and Tilly missed signs
- Ambiguous: we never quite know, but Tilly's life is changed

# Reflection

The prompt is fantastic because those three blood drop emojis are so *teenage* — the way we communicate horror and crisis in glyphs now, a whole emotional weather system compressed into pictograms. The dark comedy lives in the gap between the epic gravity the narrator feels and the potentially absurd/mundane reality, OR in the gap between the casual texture of the text and genuine horror beneath. Best British YA dark comedy (Sue Townsend, Louise O'Neill's sharper moments, Alice Oseman when she cuts) sits in that gap.

I think Plot 1 (The Night Walk) is strongest structurally for 8 chapters — it gives me a quest spine, natural chapter breaks (each "stop"), escalating stakes, room for comedy in the errors and detours, and a clear emotional arc. Plot 5 (complicity in violence) is tempting but risks tipping into thriller territory and losing the YA voice. Plot 2 (the pact) is clever but might feel too gimmicky. Plot 4 (vampire switch) is a one-note joke stretched thin.

What I want to avoid:
- Pat moralism. YA dark comedy fails when it becomes an Issue Book with jokes frosted on top. The humour has to be load-bearing, not decorative.
- Making the protagonist too passive. She needs agency, stupidity, her own flaws driving the plot.
- The "best friend in crisis, I must save her" framing being played straight. It should be complicated — maybe Tilly is a bit jealous, a bit performative, a bit thrilled to be needed. That's where the darkness in HER lives.
- Too-neat reveal. The three blood drops should resonate ambiguously even after we "know" — maybe they meant multiple things.

What excites me:
- The idea that Tilly spends the whole night constructing narratives about what happened — cycling through the possibilities (period? pregnancy? murder? self-harm?) — and each wrong guess tells us something about her. The emoji is a Rorschach for her anxieties.
- Class and setting: a specific British town. Maybe a seaside off-season town, or a northern mill town, or a commuter belt nowhere. Grey, specific, with that YA flatness that's both boring and charged.
- The best friend not being a saint. The reveal being morally messy — maybe Nora did something bad, or Nora is fine and was being melodramatic, or the truth is smaller and sadder than Tilly's imagined horrors.
- The protagonist's own secret. She's looking for Nora but we're also watching HER — perhaps she fancies Nora, or resents her, or sent a text of her own earlier that night she's trying to take back.

A promising direction: Tilly gets the text, launches into the night, and each stop she makes is both a search and a self-exposure. By the end, we've learned what happened to Nora (something real but perhaps not the apocalyptic thing Tilly imagined) AND something about Tilly that reframes the friendship. The comedy comes from Tilly's voice — sharp, deflective, occasionally cruel — and from the mundane absurdities of trying to conduct a rescue mission in a small British town at 1am (night bus doesn't come, ends up at a 24-hour Tesco, has to ask a guy from her chemistry class for help, etc.).

Ending tone: not neat. Morning light, a changed but still-here friendship, something slightly broken in Tilly that wasn't broken before, and a joke that lands with a bruise. That's the target.
step_outputs.2:
# Intention

I'm writing a darkly comic British YA short story structured as a single-night quest: sixteen-year-old Tilly receives three blood-drop emojis from her best friend Nora just after midnight, and spends the rest of the night trying to find her, cycling through increasingly baroque theories about what the message means. Each "stop" on her journey is both a search for Nora and an inadvertent exposure of Tilly herself.

**Voice & Style:** First-person present tense, Tilly narrating. Sharp, sardonic, deflective — the voice of a clever girl who weaponises wit to avoid her own feelings. Think Sue Townsend's rhythm married to a bleaker, more contemporary sensibility. British specifics are load-bearing, not decorative: night buses, Greggs, a 24-hour Tesco, UCAS forms on the bedroom floor, a stepdad asleep in front of the snooker. The town is a commuter-belt nowhere on the Kent coast — call it Saltmere — grey, off-season, full of closed amusement arcades and vape shops.

**What I'm aiming for:**
- Comedy that is load-bearing, not frosting. The jokes come from Tilly's voice, from absurd logistics, from the mismatch between her cinematic interior monologue and the tatty reality.
- An unreliable, compromised narrator. Tilly is not a saint. She's jealous of Nora, a bit in love with her, a bit thrilled to be chosen as the person who got the text. Her "rescue mission" has ego in it.
- A Rorschach structure for the emoji: Tilly projects her own anxieties onto the blood drops (murder, suicide, assault, pregnancy, occult). Each theory reveals her, not Nora.
- A reveal that's morally messy and smaller-than-expected in some ways, larger in others. Not an Issue Book tidy resolution. The truth about Nora is complicated, human, and partially mundane; but Tilly's role in the friendship is the real dark revelation.
- A final chapter that doesn't tie a bow. Morning light. A joke that bruises. Something slightly and permanently shifted.

**What I'm avoiding:**
- Pat moralism; the Issue Book tone.
- Making Nora a saintly victim or Tilly a pure rescuer.
- Neat resolution of the emoji's meaning (it should retain some ambiguity).
- Thriller escalation (no murders, no cover-ups — this is YA darkly comic, not crime).
- Twee Britishisms or cosy-gritty clichés. Specificity over texture.
- Over-explaining. Trust the reader.

**Key structural choice:** Tilly's wrong theories escalate in horror, but the truth, when it arrives, is painful in a quieter, more embarrassing, more ongoing way — the kind of bad thing that doesn't resolve, just continues. Meanwhile, Tilly's own small betrayal (something she did earlier that evening, seeded early, paid off late) is what actually damages her.

# Chapter Planning

**Chapter 1: Three Drops**
00:04. Tilly in her bedroom in Saltmere, UCAS personal statement open on her laptop, the text arrives. Establish: voice, family (mum on second marriage, stepdad Gary and his snooker), the friend group chat, Tilly's relationship with Nora — glamorous, chaotic, magnetic, Tilly's orbit. Tilly calls Nora. No answer. Texts back — read, no reply. She begins constructing theories. Decides to go out. Seeds: her phone has an unsent message to someone else; she's been drinking a bit; a passing mention of Nora's boyfriend Finn (older, works at the garage, a bit of a nothing who thinks he's something). Ends: Tilly in a hoodie, on her bike, the seafront road.

**Chapter 2: Nora's House**
Tilly bikes to Nora's. Climbs the trellis (comedy of competence — she's done it before). Nora's room: empty, bed made, the specific wrongness of a tidy teenage bedroom. Tilly snoops, finds something — a pregnancy test box in the bin, no test. Or a letter. Or a photograph that's been torn. Nora's mum half-wakes; Tilly has to hide in the wardrobe, claustrophobic comedy. Escapes. Now convinced: pregnancy. Or miscarriage. Theory one locks in. Bike towards Finn's.

**Chapter 3: The Garage Flat**
Finn lives above the garage where he works. Tilly hammers on the door. He answers in boxers, bewildered, hostile. Dark comedy of a seventeen-year-old trying to intimidate a nineteen-year-old. He hasn't seen Nora. Tilly catches a flicker — he's lying about something, but it's not what she thinks. He calls Nora a "mental case," lets slip they broke up last week. Tilly didn't know. A small wound: she's been demoted as confidante. New theory: self-harm. She bikes off fast, cruel goodbye line, immediately regrets it.

**Chapter 4: The Party That Isn't**
Tilly tries the house of Jess (third in their friend group). Jess is having a tiny pre-exam gathering — four people, a bottle of Lambrini, a vape. Tilly arrives frantic. They haven't seen Nora. Jess's response is odd — defensive, shifty. Tilly, rattled, drinks too fast, accuses Jess of something. The group dynamics crack open: Tilly realises she hasn't been paying attention; Nora and Jess have been closer lately; something's been going on in the group she missed. Chemistry-class boy Ollie is there — awkward, sweet. He offers to help look. Tilly, humiliated, accepts. They leave on foot.

**Chapter 5: The Seafront at 2am**
Tilly and Ollie walk the front looking for Nora. The closed arcades, the pier, the shuttered chip shop. Comedy of their halting conversation over genuine dread. Tilly constructs her worst theory: the sea. Ollie is decent, steady, says the right unhelpful things. Tilly snaps at him. They find Nora's jacket on a bench. Not her — just her jacket. Tilly nearly breaks. Ollie calls the non-emergency line. Tilly remembers something — a place Nora mentioned once, a specific spot.

**Chapter 6: The Allotments**
The allotments at the edge of town where Nora's granddad used to have a shed before he died. Tilly finds Nora there, alive, sitting on the shed floor, wrapped in a blanket, eating a Twix. Anticlimax. Rage floods Tilly. Then the real conversation: Nora's mum's new boyfriend has been — the detail is kept small, specific, awful but not lurid — doing things. Looking at her. Moving things in her room. Nothing "bad enough" to act on. Nora sent the text because she'd started her period in the shed and it felt like the only honest thing she could say. Three drops. Tilly sits down. The reveal isn't a single event — it's an ongoing, unresolvable situation Nora has been carrying. And she told Jess first, weeks ago. That's the real bruise.

**Chapter 7: What Tilly Did**
They walk back as the sky greys. Tilly confesses — not to Nora, but to the reader, and obliquely to Nora — what she did earlier that night: she sent a message to someone (a boy Nora liked, or a teacher, or posted something in the group) that was petty and damaging, from a place of feeling sidelined. Payoff of the Chapter 1 seed. She can't take it back. Nora either finds out in real time (phone pings) or doesn't — I'll decide in drafting, but I'm leaning toward *doesn't yet*, which is worse. They reach Nora's house. Nora goes inside. Tilly bikes home in the dawn.

**Chapter 8: Monday**
Jump forward: Monday morning, school. The group chat is quiet. Nora is off. Jess won't look at Tilly. The message Tilly sent has landed and is doing its slow damage. A scene with Ollie that is small and decent and inadequate. A final moment with Nora — a corridor, a look, one line of dialogue that is both a joke and not. Tilly alone, walking home past the seafront. The three drops mean something different now — not catastrophe, but the quiet accumulation of things that don't resolve. The story ends on a joke that bruises: something flip Tilly says out loud to no one, that lands as grief.
step_outputs.3:
# How a Human Writer Might Approach This

A human writer — particularly one working in British YA dark comedy — would likely start from voice before plot. They'd hear Tilly in their head, maybe based on a real teenager they know or were, and let the plot fall out of that voice's particular rhythms and blind spots. The three-blood-drops prompt would probably make them laugh first, then wince. They'd think about their own midnight texts, their own group chats, the specific embarrassment of being sixteen and thinking everything is life-or-death because sometimes it actually is.

A human would likely:
- Let scenes run long when they're alive and cut them brutally short when they're not, regardless of "chapter balance."
- Include details that serve no plot function but are *true* — a specific song playing, a weird thing a parent says, the exact texture of a half-eaten Twix.
- Let characters be inconsistent in ways that feel right rather than ways that telegraph theme.
- Trust the reader enough to leave gaps, mysteries, unexplained behaviours.
- Write the jokes that actually make them laugh, not the jokes that "fit the tone."
- Be willing to have the story *not quite work* in places, as long as it's alive.
- Draw from specific embarrassments and cruelties they've actually committed or witnessed.
- Let the ending disappoint itself a little — because real endings do.

# Telltale LLM Approaches (and Why They'd Hurt This Piece)

**1. Thematic over-signalling.** LLMs love to make every detail *mean* something. Every prop is a symbol, every minor character delivers a thematic lesson, every chapter ends on a line that telegraphs its meaning. This piece needs *slack* — details that are just details, scenes that don't quite resolve, jokes that don't have thematic weight.

**2. Symmetrical structure.** LLMs tend to make chapters the same size, give every setup a payoff, mirror the opening in the closing. Real stories are lumpy. The best YA dark comedy is often structurally off-kilter.

**3. The "literary" register creeping in.** When LLMs try to write well, they reach for a certain mid-literary voice: careful metaphors, balanced sentences, decorative observation. Tilly needs to sound like a pissed-off sixteen-year-old, not like someone auditioning for the Guardian.

**4. Emotional legibility.** LLMs tend to explain feelings either directly ("she felt a pang of jealousy") or via heavy-handed imagery. Teenagers don't know what they feel, and they especially don't *name* it. Keep emotions tangled, misdirected, displaced.

**5. Bow-tying.** LLMs find it genuinely hard to leave things unresolved. Even when instructed to, they tend to resolve *something* — a character lesson, a thematic statement, a hopeful note. The pull toward closure is strong.

**6. Safety around the hard stuff.** LLMs soften. The stepdad situation in Chapter 6 — there's a risk it gets treated with either gingerly distance or a strange reverence that kills the humour. Real dark comedy doesn't treat trauma as sacred; it treats it as part of life, alongside everything else, which is what gives it its sting.

**7. Over-explanation.** LLMs fill in. They explain jokes, unpack metaphors, clarify motivations. British comedy particularly runs on implication, understatement, the unsaid.

**8. Generic specificity.** LLMs reach for specificity but often pick generic-specific items — a "Twix," a "Greggs" — from a mental list of British signifiers rather than the truly telling detail. The difference between a writer who actually knows the bus number and one who just says "the night bus" is palpable.

**9. Exposition in dialogue.** LLMs use dialogue to deliver information. Real teenagers talk past each other, misunderstand, drop threads, repeat themselves, reference shared history without explaining it.

**10. Moral protagonist.** Even when told to write a flawed protagonist, LLMs tend to soften her flaws or make them redeemable. Tilly needs to be genuinely a bit of a shit.

# Critique of the Current Plan

**The Intention document itself has LLM fingerprints.** The tidy bulleted "aiming for / avoiding" lists, the confident tone, the way every choice is justified — this reads like a writer who has already made the story safe by fully understanding it. Real writing surprises the writer.

**Specific concerns with the plan:**

**Chapter structure is too neat.** Eight chapters, each a "stop" on a quest, each roughly a thousand words, each advancing the plot by one clean beat. Real rambling-nocturnal-quest stories are messier. Some stops should be duds. Some should be too long. Chapter 2 (Nora's house), Chapter 3 (Finn's flat), Chapter 4 (the party) — these are basically the same shape: Tilly arrives, learns something, updates theory, leaves. Risk of monotony.

**The Chekhov's Gun of "what Tilly did" is very LLM.** The plan seeds something in Chapter 1 and pays it off in Chapter 7. This is structural tidiness pretending to be messiness. A human might have Tilly do something terrible *during* the night, out of the chaos of the night, not have it already loaded before the text arrives. Or — more radically — the thing she did might not pay off at all, might just sit there.

**The reveal in Chapter 6 is doing too much work.** Nora's situation (stepdad-adjacent creepiness, ongoing, unresolvable) + "she told Jess first" + the period detail explaining the emoji — that's three reveals stacked. Each one softens the others. A human writer might pick one and let it land harder, or let the reveal be even smaller and more baffling.

**The Ollie character risks being a functional device.** "Awkward, sweet, decent." He helps Tilly, she snaps at him, he's steady. This is the YA-sidekick-boy archetype. Either make him weirder, more complicit, more off, or cut him and let Tilly be alone for more of the night.

**The "Rorschach" theory-cycling is a clever idea that could become mechanical.** If each chapter has Tilly locking in a new theory and then having it disproved, readers will see the pattern by Chapter 3 and start waiting for it. The wrong theories need to feel more organic and less schematic — some should overlap, some should be half-held, some should be abandoned mid-chapter without resolution.

**The ending is too designed.** "A joke that bruises" is a lovely phrase but it's also a recipe. The risk is I'll write toward that pre-planned effect rather than discovering the actual ending. The final line will probably come out sounding writerly and self-aware rather than accidentally devastating.

**The setting (Saltmere, Kent coast) is pre-fabricated.** I named it, I gave it the "closed amusement arcades" treatment, and it's already threatening to become Generic British Coastal Sadness. The seafront walk in Chapter 5 particularly risks this — "the closed arcades, the pier, the shuttered chip shop" is an LLM postcard.

**The "theme" is visible.** The plan clearly wants to be about: friendship as ego, the limits of performative rescue, trauma that doesn't resolve, being sixteen and self-obsessed. These are legible themes from the outside. A human writer often doesn't know their theme until they've finished. The visible theme makes every scene's *purpose* legible, which kills mystery.

**The voice description is on-the-nose.** "Sardonic, deflective, a clever girl who weaponises wit to avoid her own feelings" — this is also the description of approximately every YA dark-comedy narrator. The voice needs a particular crack in it, some distinctive verbal tic or blind spot that isn't just "sarcastic teen."

# Ideas to Make It More Human

**Voice-level:**
- Give Tilly a specific verbal tic or vocabulary quirk — maybe she uses a particular word wrong, or has a catchphrase from a TV show no one else watches, or narrates in a specific register borrowed from somewhere (true crime podcasts, her mum's language, a book she loves).
- Let her lie to the reader. Not in a big twist way — in small, embarrassed ways. "I wasn't crying" when she clearly was.
- Let her be boring sometimes. Not every line needs to crackle.
- Let her be stupider than the reader occasionally — miss things we see.
- Let her be funnier than the plan suggests, but also less funny when she's trying hardest.

**Structural:**
- Let a chapter be almost nothing. A non-event. Tilly sits at a bus stop for ten minutes. Real nights have dead time.
- Let a chapter's drama be unrelated to Nora — a random encounter, a weird stranger, a fox, a fight in a kebab shop she watches — that changes Tilly without advancing "the plot."
- Consider breaking time in one chapter — a flashback to a specific memory with Nora that contradicts Tilly's current narrative about the friendship.
- Don't let every chapter end on a "beat." Let some just stop.

**Plot-level:**
- The truth about Nora could be genuinely small. Not "ongoing stepdad situation" but something like: she had a panic attack, she hates her life, she doesn't know why she sent it. The three drops meaning nothing coherent. This is more honest to teenage crisis than a Reveal.
- Or: the truth is worse and simpler than the plan. Or worse and weirder.
- Consider: Tilly never finds Nora. The story ends with her still not knowing. Nora turns up fine on Monday with no explanation.
- Consider: Tilly finds Nora and Nora is annoyed she came.
- The "thing Tilly did earlier" — either cut it entirely, or make it discovered in the middle and unresolved, or have it turn out smaller than she thought.

**Character-level:**
- Make Tilly's love for Nora more complicated — not coded romantic, or coded romantic in a way Tilly refuses to name, or actively contemptuous in places. Real intense teenage friendships have hate in them.
- Make Nora less luminous. The plan describes her as "glamorous, chaotic, magnetic" — this is Tilly's view, but the reader should see cracks. Maybe Nora is actually a bit boring. Maybe she's mean. Maybe she's the less interesting of the two and Tilly has built a cult around her.
- Let the parents be weirder. Gary the stepdad asleep in front of the snooker is a stock image. What if he's awake? What if he's kind? What if he's the one Tilly actually confides in at the end?

**Detail-level:**
- The physical geography needs to be specific in a way that only works if I actually map it. Names of streets. The specific chain — is the kebab shop called anything in particular? Does the night bus actually run in Saltmere? (Maybe it doesn't, and that's the joke — she can't get anywhere.)
- Pick details that *resist* meaning. A song Tilly hates is stuck in her head. A weird ad on a bus shelter. A pigeon with a missing foot. Stuff that doesn't symbolise anything.
- Weather should not be pathetic-fallacy-ing. If it rains, it rains at the wrong time, or stops at the wrong time, or never rains at all.

**Tonal:**
- Let something be genuinely unfunny. Let a joke fall flat on the page — Tilly makes a joke, no one laughs, she feels it.
- Let Tilly be afraid in a way that isn't stylised. Just scared, stupidly, like a kid.
- The dark comedy should sometimes just be dark, or just be comedy. Not always both at once.

**Ending:**
- Resist the "joke that bruises" formula. The ending might be a non-joke. Or a real joke that's just funny. Or silence.
- Don't make Monday do too much work. Consider ending on Sunday evening, or Tuesday lunch, or a week later in a specific trivial moment.
- Let the three blood drops retain some mystery forever. Tilly might never ask Nora what they meant. That's more true than the neat explanation.

# Intention

A single-night story in eight chapters: Tilly, sixteen, gets three blood-drop emojis from her best friend Nora just after midnight and goes out into a small Kent commuter town to find her. The story is what happens in the next six hours, and then a coda.

**Voice.** First person, present tense, Tilly. Her specific verbal tic: she narrates in the cadence of the true-crime podcasts she listens to while falling asleep — "the last known sighting," "in hindsight," "what she didn't know was" — borrowed gravitas applied to her own life. This is partly funny, partly a real way of coping, and partly the mechanism by which she keeps missing what's in front of her. She should also be allowed to be unfunny, to drop the bit, to be scared in a plain way. She lies to the reader in small, embarrassed ways. She uses one word wrong consistently (I'll pick in drafting — maybe "literally" in a way even she'd mock in someone else, or a malapropism she's committed to).

**Nora.** Not luminous. The plan previously had her as glamorous and magnetic; that's Tilly's framing, and the reader should feel the framing strain. Nora is actually a bit boring, a bit mean, sometimes funny. Tilly has built a cult around her because Tilly needs to be near someone who seems to know what she's doing. Nora doesn't know what she's doing.

**The truth about the three drops.** I'm going smaller and weirder than the previous plan. Nora doesn't have a hidden trauma the story is going to unveil. She had a bad night — a row with her mum, a panic attack, a broken-up-with boyfriend, started her period unexpectedly in a place with no loo roll, and sent the text because it was the one honest thing she could type. The three drops don't mean one thing. They mean several small things at once, and also nothing. This is more true to teenage crisis than a Reveal. The darkness in the story comes from Tilly's response to this — her disappointment that it isn't bigger, her performance of concern, and the thing she does with that disappointment.

**What Tilly does.** Not pre-seeded in Chapter 1. It happens *during* the night, out of frustration and ego, somewhere around Chapter 4 or 5 — she does something petty online (posts something, forwards a screenshot, says something cruel in the group chat thinking Nora won't see) and it sits there unresolved. By the final chapter it may or may not have detonated. I won't confirm for the reader that it has.

**Structural looseness.** Not every chapter advances the plot. One chapter is a dead stop — a long wait, a strange encounter that goes nowhere. Chapters vary in pace. Some end on a beat, some just stop. The theory-cycling (Tilly's wrong theories about the emoji) is present but not schematic — sometimes overlapping, sometimes half-abandoned, sometimes she forgets what she thought ten minutes ago.

**What I'm avoiding.**
- Pre-fabricated British Coastal Sadness. The town is specific, named (Saltmere), but I'll resist the postcard (pier, arcades, chip shop) and go for the odder detail.
- Ollie as functional sidekick. He's cut, or reduced to a cameo.
- The Reveal as the story's engine. The engine is Tilly's voice and the gap between her narration and what's happening.
- Thematic signalling. No lines that announce the theme.
- A tidy ending. The ending is small, trivial, and unresolved.
- Making Nora's situation a lurid trauma. Her bad night is a bad night. Plenty.
- Pathetic fallacy. The weather is boring.

**What I'm aiming for.** A story that's funny, often, in a specific teenage way; that makes the reader uncomfortable with how much they like Tilly; that ends without ceremony; where the three blood drops retain some mystery even for the characters involved.

# Chapter Planning

**Chapter 1: 00:04**
Tilly in her bedroom. The text arrives. Establish: voice, the true-crime cadence, the UCAS draft, the sound of Gary's snooker downstairs, her mum's laugh. The group chat is called something stupid. Tilly's immediate reaction is not worry but a small, private thrill — she got the text. She tries calling. No answer. She texts back, watches it go read. She starts constructing theories, narrating them in podcast voice. She makes a decision to go out that she frames as heroic but is partly because she was bored, partly because she wants the story of having gone. She puts on eyeliner before she leaves. Ends: the front door, quietly.

**Chapter 2: The Bike**
Saltmere at midnight. Tilly on her bike. This chapter is mostly movement and interior — the town's specific geography, the one takeaway still open, a man she half-knows smoking outside it who doesn't recognise her. She goes to Nora's. The trellis routine, but tonight it's wet and she nearly falls. Nora's room is empty and too tidy. She doesn't find a pregnancy test. She finds something smaller and weirder: Nora's phone, face down on the pillow. This is wrong. No teenager leaves without their phone. Tilly takes it. Nora's mum calls out from the landing; Tilly freezes, then escapes. In the street, she can't unlock the phone. Bikes off. New theory: something happened *to* Nora, she didn't send the text — someone did.

**Chapter 3: Finn**
Finn's flat above the garage. He answers in tracksuit bottoms. The scene is shorter and nastier than I'd previously planned — Finn is not a villain, he's just a nineteen-year-old who's been dumped and is embarrassed to be at home. He tells Tilly they broke up eight days ago. Tilly didn't know. The small wound: she hasn't actually spoken to Nora properly in nearly a fortnight. He says Nora's been "a bit all over the place." He's not hostile, which is worse. He offers her tea. She refuses and leaves. On the step she cries for a minute, surprises herself, stops. New confusion: if they broke up a week ago, why did Tilly still think of Nora as someone with a boyfriend? Because Nora didn't tell her.

**Chapter 4: Jess's Kitchen**
Tilly goes to Jess's — the third friend. Not a party, just Jess and one other girl, Mira, eating toast at 1am. Jess is surprised to see Tilly. The conversation is stilted in a way Tilly initially reads as guilt but is actually just Jess being tired and slightly uninterested. Tilly shows them the text. Jess says, "Oh, she does that," which lands like a slap. *Does that.* Tilly realises Nora has sent other people the blood drops before, or something like them. She's not special. She's not the person Nora turned to. She was just the one awake. Tilly, humiliated, says something cutting about Jess's boyfriend. Leaves. In the street, she opens the group chat — not the main one, the one without Nora — and posts a screenshot of something. I'll decide the content in drafting; it should be small, petty, recognisable as the kind of thing you do when you're hurt. This is the thing she does. She doesn't immediately regret it.

**Chapter 5: The Bus Shelter**
The dead-stop chapter. Tilly waits at a bus shelter for a bus that isn't coming — she's forgotten the night buses don't run on Sundays in Saltmere, or only go one way. She sits for a long time. An older woman is also there, drunk, friendly, chatty, not threatening, not a life-lesson-deliverer. They talk about nothing. The woman eats chips out of paper. Tilly tries three more times to unlock Nora's phone. Fails. She thinks about going home. She doesn't. This chapter moves no plot. It should feel like the actual middle of the night — slow, cold, a bit funny, a bit dreadful. At the end, she remembers the allotments. Nora's granddad's shed. She walks.

**Chapter 6: The Shed**
She finds Nora. Alive, sitting inside the shed, wrapped in a coat, phone-less (obviously), a bit damp. The scene is not a Reveal. It's two sixteen-year-olds in a shed at two in the morning, and one of them is annoyed the other came. Nora's explanation, delivered over the course of the chapter in pieces and evasions: she had a massive row with her mum; she walked out; she came here because she used to come here; she started her period and had nothing with her; her phone was dead anyway (Tilly doesn't mention she has it); she sent the text from the last 3% of battery because she couldn't think of words. Was she going to do something bad? She looks at Tilly like that's a stupid question, then says, "I don't know. Probably not." Tilly wants it to be bigger. She is ashamed of wanting it to be bigger. She gives Nora her jumper. They sit in the shed. Nora says, "Why are you here?" — not cruelly, just asking. Tilly doesn't have a good answer.

**Chapter 7: Walking Back**
Pre-dawn. They walk back through Saltmere. The chapter is mostly small talk with long silences. Tilly keeps not giving Nora her phone back; she'll give it to her at the door, she decides, then doesn't. The thing Tilly posted earlier is still out there; her own phone buzzes and she doesn't look. Nora talks about something trivial for a long time — a show, a teacher, nothing to do with the night. Tilly realises she doesn't actually know Nora very well. At Nora's gate they hug in a way that isn't quite right. Nora goes in. Tilly puts the phone through the letterbox. Bikes home. Gary is awake in the kitchen, making toast. He says, "Alright, love." She says, "Alright." She goes to bed in her clothes.

**Chapter 8: Tuesday**
Skip Monday. Tuesday lunchtime, school canteen. The thing Tilly posted has done its small damage — not catastrophic, just sour. Jess isn't speaking to her. Nora is, sort of — they sit together at lunch but don't really talk. Nora is eating a Twix. Tilly wants to ask about the three drops and doesn't. A boy Tilly barely knows says something stupid at their table and Nora laughs, and Tilly laughs, and for a second it's fine. Then it isn't. The final beat is small: Tilly walks home alone past the allotments, sees the shed from the road, and keeps walking. She makes a joke out loud, to herself, about something unrelated. It isn't funny. She says it again, slightly different, trying to get it to land. It doesn't. End.

**Background.** Sixteen, just finished Year 12. Lives with her mum Deb and stepdad Gary in a three-bed semi on the newer side of Saltmere — the side built in 2003, the side without sea views. She listens to true-crime podcasts to fall asleep. She has listened to hundreds of hours of women being murdered, narrated by two women in Wisconsin called Marcie and Bree. She has absorbed their cadences completely. She doesn't know she's doing it.

She misses things constantly, particularly things that would require revising her sense of her own importance. She is jealous in small specific ways: when Nora mentions someone Tilly doesn't know, when Jess texts Nora without copying her in, when a teacher singles out someone else's essay. She is also genuinely funny, genuinely loving, and genuinely brave in the actual moment — she does get on her bike at midnight, she does climb the trellis. The problem is what she does with it afterwards, the story she tells herself about having done it.

# Chapter 1: 00:04

The last known sighting of Nora Whitlock was Sunday afternoon, 3:47pm, at the benches outside Costa — a blurred photo on her story, holding a can of something pink, laughing at someone off-camera. She has not posted since. She has not been seen in public since. The subject was last in contact with her friends via a Snapchat of her own foot in a sock at 9:12pm.

I'm doing the voice again. I know. I can hear it.

The thing is, it started as a joke. Marcie and Bree do this thing where they say *the subject was last in contact* in these very calm Wisconsin voices, and then they tell you the woman's dead. I started narrating my own life like that about a year ago, in my head, because it was funny, because nothing ever happens in Saltmere, because saying *the subject was last seen eating a Pret baguette at Ashford International* is funnier than saying *I had a sandwich on the train*. And now I can't stop. It's like a song you've learned wrong. It's the cadence I think in.

It's 00:04. I'm on my bed, laptop open to the UCAS personal statement I have rewritten nine times. The current opening is: *I have always believed that literature is a form of listening.* Even I can tell it's terrible. I can hear Gary downstairs, which means the snooker is on, which means he's asleep in front of the snooker, which means my mum is in bed because the laugh I heard through the wall earlier was her on the phone to her sister Karen, which — not that Karen. Different Karen. God, there are too many Karens.

The phone goes. Not rings. Buzzes once, the soft one, a text.

🩸🩸🩸

No words. No name — but I don't need the name, because I have Nora's number memorised the way you memorise your own, and I can see Nora Whitlock at the top of the screen before I've fully registered what I'm looking at.

I sit up. Then I lie down again, because for about three seconds my actual feeling is — and I'm going to be honest here, because there's no point not being honest — *she picked me.*

It's midnight. Nora has sent me three blood drops at midnight. Three. Blood drops. At midnight. Out of all the people in her phone, she has chosen me, Matilda Brennan, Year 12, bedroom of, and she has sent me the most cryptic and dramatic communication of my entire life, and the correct response, I understand, the *human* response, is to feel afraid.

I do feel afraid. Eventually. After the other thing.

I call her. Straight to voicemail, the one where she's doing a posh voice. I hang up halfway through *frightfully busy.* I text back: *??* Then: *u ok.* Then, because the ?? and the u ok look like something a mother would send: *NORA.*

Read. 00:06. 00:07. 00:08.

I sit with the phone face-up on my stomach and I run the theories, because that's what I do. Marcie and Bree would call it *triage.* I call it triage.

Theory one: she's pregnant. But blood drops aren't pregnancy. Pregnancy would be the little pink bow. Or — I don't know. There isn't a pregnancy emoji. There might be. I don't check.

Theory two: she's *lost* the pregnancy. Literally — and I know, *literally* — three drops, three stages, one for each, like stations of the cross. This feels cinematic enough to be true. I hold it for eleven seconds.

Theory three: she's hurt herself. This one I don't let myself look at directly. It sits at the edge of the screen like a pop-up.

Theory four: someone else is hurt. Finn. Her mum. Stuart, the boyfriend of her mum, who is boring but has hands and a car.

Theory five: it's a prank. Nora does pranks. Nora once sent me a picture of herself in an ambulance and it turned out she was in the back of her cousin's Vauxhall Corsa with the light on. Nora has form.

Theory six: it's a cry for help in the actual clinical sense and I am currently wasting time making it about emojis.

I sit up properly. I put the phone down. I pick it up. I call her again. Voicemail. I don't leave one.

The thing about the subject — about Nora — is that she's chaotic. She *is* chaotic. I've built a whole cathedral to her chaos. I have been, for two years now, the person who tells stories about Nora at parties: *oh my god, you'll love this, Nora once* — and I am so used to being that person that it takes me until 00:14 to notice that the last time Nora actually phoned me was September. That the last time we spent an evening alone, just us, no Jess, no one's boyfriend, no group, was August. That I don't actually know, at this exact minute, where she has been for the past four hours.

This is the kind of thing you notice in hindsight, Marcie would say, and Bree would agree, and then they would play an advert for mattresses.

I get up. I put on jeans. I put on my good coat — the wool one, not the parka — because if I'm going to be the person who went out at midnight to find her best friend, I want to look like that person and not like someone doing the bins. I do my eyeliner. This takes four minutes. I don't think about why I'm doing it.

Downstairs, Gary's snoring. The snooker is on a break. Two men in waistcoats are discussing the green. I put my key in my pocket, lift my bike off the wall, carry it through the kitchen because the shed key is lost, and open the front door with my elbow.

The street is empty. The air smells of the sea and of someone's bonfire from earlier.

I get on the bike.

*The subject,* I think, *left the property at approximately 00:19, alone.*

# Chapter 2: The Bike

Saltmere at midnight looks like Saltmere at six in the evening, except emptier and with the streetlights doing that orange thing where everyone's skin would look dead if there were anyone around to check.

I go down Mercer Road, which is the fast way, then cut through the alley behind the Co-op, which is the faster way and also the way you are not supposed to go alone. The Co-op has a security light that comes on when you pass the bins and turns you, for about four seconds, into the main character of a film about a missing girl.

I am aware of how this looks. I am aware that I am both the person doing the looking and the person who might be looked at. This is the problem with the Marcie and Bree voice: you're always, at some level, casting yourself.

Nadim's is still open, which surprises me. Nadim's is never open past eleven. Through the window I can see one man, not Nadim, leaning on the counter watching something on his phone. Outside, on the bench, there's a bloke I half-know — one of Gary's Wednesday-league darts friends, or maybe it's his son — smoking and looking at his shoes. He glances up when I go past. He doesn't clock me. I am, to him, a girl on a bike. I am, in this moment, nobody.

This is new. I don't think I've been nobody, in Saltmere, since I was about eight.

Nora's is a ten-minute ride. I do it in seven, standing up on the pedals for the hill on Granville Road, and I arrive sweating in my good coat and not thinking about that yet because the house is dark, both floors, even the landing light that Karen leaves on for Stuart when he's on a late shift.

I push the bike behind the hedge. I check the street. I check it again, because Marcie and Bree would want me to. I go round the side.

The trellis routine, when Nora's awake and waiting, takes about thirty seconds and involves me getting a leg-up from the bin and her hauling me in through the window while whispering *for god's sake Tilly*. Tonight, alone, in the wet, it takes eleven minutes and I nearly fall twice. The trellis is one of those diamond wooden ones that isn't meant for weight. The second time I nearly fall I say *shit* out loud and then clamp my mouth shut because Karen's bedroom is directly below and Karen sleeps like an animal on alert.

I get in.

Nora's room.

Here is what I know about Nora's room: there is always washing on the chair, there is always a mug on the desk with something growing in it, there are always three or four books open face-down on the floor in a radius around the bed, like she fell asleep mid-reading-four-books, which is a lie she wants to be true about herself. There are fairy lights she bought at a festival that only half work. There is a poster of Patti Smith she got because Jess had one and Jess got one because some boy Jess fancied had one. There is the mug — *the* mug, the one with the rude cartoon, from Ray — on the shelf.

Tonight.

The bed is made.

I stand in the middle of the carpet, dripping, and I can't work out for about ten seconds what's wrong, and then I realise it's that. The bed is made. Nora's bed has not been made since Nora was in primary school. The duvet is pulled flat. The pillow is squared up. The books on the floor have been stacked. The washing has gone.

This is the room of someone who has tidied before leaving. This is — Marcie and Bree would say — *a scene that had been prepared.*

I stop.

I think: *suicide note.*

I don't find a suicide note. I find a phone.

Her phone. Face-down, dead centre of the pillow, like it's been placed there. I turn it over. The screen is black. I press the button. Nothing. I press it harder. A battery icon appears, almost empty, one red line. It's dying. It's nearly dead.

No one leaves without their phone. No sixteen-year-old girl I have ever met, including Nora, including especially Nora, leaves a house without her phone. Your phone is the thing you take when the building is on fire. Your phone is the thing you take before your shoes.

I pick it up. I try to unlock it. I try her birthday. I try 0000. I try 1234. It tells me to try again in one minute.

Downstairs, the landing creaks.

"Nora?" — Karen's voice, low, muzzy. Not fully awake. The voice of a woman who has heard something and is deciding whether to commit to having heard it.

I go into the wardrobe.

I have been in Nora's wardrobe before, twice, both times with Nora in it with me, both times drunk. Alone and sober and with another person's phone in my hand, it is a different experience. I close the door with one finger and I stand in the dark among her dresses and I hold my breath until my chest hurts.

I wait four minutes. I count them.

I climb out of the wardrobe. I climb out of the window. I get back on the bike.

Her phone is in my pocket. Mine is in my other pocket. The two of them knock together as I pedal.

New theory. Brand new theory, slotting in over all the others like a top card.

She didn't send the text.

There's no being subtle about it.

*Hi Finn, have you murdered my friend.* No.

*Hi Finn, did you send a text from my friend's phone while she was dead in a canal.* Also no, and also she wasn't in a canal, because she was in her bedroom tidying, and also her phone is in my pocket, so.

The new theory, the someone-else-sent-it theory, has already started to fall apart on the bike over here, because if someone else sent it they'd have taken the phone, wouldn't they, they wouldn't have left it face-down on the pillow like a calling card. Unless they wanted it to look like she'd left it. Unless they were clever. Finn is not clever. Finn came second to bottom in GCSE Maths, according to Nora, who told me this like it was evidence of his charm.

I knock.

Nothing. I knock again, harder, with the flat of my hand. I hear movement. I hear a voice, male, muffled, going *for fuck's sake.* I hear the lock.

Finn opens the door.

His eyes are red and squinted half-shut against the stairwell bulb, and for a second he looks at me like he genuinely doesn't know who I am, and then he does, and his whole face goes through this little sequence — confusion, recognition, a flicker of *oh god what now*, and then, weirdly, concern.

"Til?"

"Where is she."

"What?"

"Where is she, Finn."

He looks behind me down the stairs, like maybe I've brought someone. Then he looks at me properly. His mouth opens. Closes. Opens.

"It's — what time is it?"

"Half twelve."

"Right." He scratches the back of his neck. "Right. Who?"

I stare at him.

I had, I realise, expected him to know who. I had expected him to say *Nora* before I did. Him not saying Nora first is so unexpected that for a second my mouth won't make the word.

"Nora," I say.

He blinks. "Nora."

"*Yes.*"

"Til, Nora's not — Nora's not here."

"Where is she."

"I don't know where she is."

"Finn."

"I don't *know*, Til, I haven't — " He stops. He steps back from the door a bit. "Come in for a second, it's — you're letting all the heat out."

"I'm not coming in."

"Then I'm letting all the heat out. Come in. Jesus. It's freezing." He turns and walks back inside and leaves the door open, which is the most effective thing he could have done, because now I'm the one being weird if I stand on the landing.

"She didn't."

"Oh."

There is a pause in which I can hear the fridge.

"Oh," he says again. "Shit. Okay. Yeah. Sorry."

"What for."

"I don't know. For — I don't know." He rubs his face. "I thought you knew."

I feel the sweat from the bike ride cooling on the back of my neck and I feel the wool of my good coat starting to smell faintly of wet dog and I feel, I realise, about to cry, which is so uncalled for and unserious that I actually get angry about it, at myself, inside my own head, in Marcie's voice. *The subject, for reasons unclear, began to get emotional in a mechanic's kitchen.*

"She alright?" he says.

"What?"

"Nora. Is she alright."

"I don't know."

"Has she — "

"I don't know, Finn."

"D'you want tea? I can do tea."

"No."

"Toast? I've got — "

"No."

"Right."

"Tell her I said." He stops. "Actually don't."

"Okay."

I turn around and go out of his flat and down the ringing staircase and onto my bike and round the corner of the garage and then I stop, and I put my feet down, and I cry for exactly one minute by the clock on Nora's dead phone, which I've taken out of my pocket for no reason, and then I stop, and I wipe my face on my sleeve, and I get back on the bike.

Week Tuesday.

Nine days.

I didn't know.

*u up*

*I'm outside*

Three dots. Then: *…what*

"Okay."

Nothing comes out.
