# Intention

This is a possession horror about a marriage already in trouble before the thing inside it was ever named. The prompt — *I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping* — is about the cowardice of pretending not to see. That cowardice is the story's real engine. The narrator is being hollowed out, yes, but he was hollowing himself out first; the entity found room because he made room. His wife, Maren, has known longer than he has and has said nothing, for reasons that are partly love and partly something harder to name.

**Plot choices:**
- Two-hander. Isolated rural house. Six months in, post-something-that-broke-them. I'll keep the rupture vague — not a miscarriage specifically, but a failure between them the reader understands by texture, not by named event.
- No locked drawer, no evidence hunt, no clean reveal scene. What Maren knows comes out sideways, in fragments, in things she doesn't finish saying. The narrator fills in wrong answers and we watch him do it.
- The entity is never explained, never named, never given rules. It is a hunger that uses the shape of a marriage.
- Maren is not a saint. She is sharp, funny in a way that wounds, capable of withholding. She has been watching him sleep because she can't stand to watch him awake. That's closer to the truth than protection.
- The narrator is not sympathetic in a simple way. He is avoidant, passive, self-pitying. The horror works because he was a good host before the thing ever arrived.
- Commit to an ending. No held breath. She does something specific in the final chapter, and it has a cost.

**Voice and style:**
- First person, past tense. Close, confessional, slightly unreliable but not theatrically so — the unreliability is the ordinary kind, the kind anyone has.
- Short paragraphs, varied sentence length. Willing to be plain. Willing to be ugly. Not reaching for the literary register; letting it arrive only when earned.
- Dialogue sparse and often evasive. People talk around things.
- Specific, weird, non-occult details over generic horror signifiers. No salt lines, no Latin, no dried flowers in drawers.
- At least one chapter where the plot barely moves. At least one moment of physical wrongness that is not ambient — something the body does that the mind can't lie about.

**What I'm avoiding:**
- The mirrored final line. The opening beat will echo, but obliquely, not as a perfect inversion.
- A scene where Maren sits down and explains the history of the entity.
- A grief backstory with a named cause.
- Tidy symbolism. Details that all pay off. A tooth in a drawer.
- "Tasteful" restraint that becomes inert. I want at least one scene that is genuinely uncomfortable.
- A clean revelation chapter. Understanding should arrive in pieces, some of them wrong.

# Chapter Planning

**Chapter 1 — Vigil**
Open on the prompt. He wakes in the dark and she is looking at him. He keeps his breathing even. He has done this four or five times now. He doesn't confront her; he waits her out, and eventually she lies down again, and he lies awake until the window greys. The chapter is almost entirely in that bed, in that held body. Small domestic context bleeds in — the house they moved to, the way they have stopped touching, the fact that he is relieved when she leaves the room. End of chapter: morning. She asks if he slept well. He says yes. First lie of the day, casually told, a habit older than whatever is happening now.

**Chapter 2 — The Honey**
A day. Not much happens. She makes him eat a spoonful of honey every morning — has for months — and he has never asked why, and he still doesn't. He works from the kitchen table. She is outside doing something with the garden he doesn't understand. He notices he has been sitting with his hand on the same page for an unknown amount of time. A phone call with his brother: the brother says *you sound like yourself again*, and it lands wrong, because he doesn't feel like himself, and also because *again* implies a before he can't locate. The chapter ends with him catching sight of her through the window, standing very still, looking at the house — not at him, at the house — and something in his chest goes quiet in a way he mistakes for peace.

**Chapter 3 — Small Cruelty**
A memory chapter, folded into a present scene. They are eating dinner. She says something that is almost a joke and almost not. He remembers a fight from a year ago — not the subject, just the shape of it, and a thing he said that he has never taken back and she has never brought up. The not-bringing-it-up is its own weather in the house. That night he dreams he is counting her ribs. He wakes with his hand on her side, and she is awake, and she doesn't move, and neither does he, and they lie there in the dark pretending to be asleep at each other. The horror here is recognisable to anyone who has been in a long relationship.

**Chapter 4 — The Thing His Body Did**
Midday. He is alone in the house. He walks into the bathroom and stands at the mirror and watches himself, for a stretch of time he cannot account for, smile. Not grimace, not twitch. Smile. A real one, the kind that uses the eyes. He is not smiling on purpose. When it stops he sits on the edge of the tub and shakes. He doesn't tell her. When she comes in from outside he can't look at her, and she notices, and she doesn't ask. The not-asking is the most frightening thing that has happened to him. End of chapter: he tries to say something at dinner and finds he has forgotten what he meant to say, completely, as if the sentence was taken out of him.

**Chapter 5 — What She Almost Says**
He tries, finally, to ask her. Not directly — he isn't capable of direct. He asks if she's been sleeping. She says *not really*. He asks if she's all right. She looks at him for a long time and says *are you*. He says yes. She says *okay*. That is the whole conversation. Later, washing dishes, she says, without looking at him, *I used to hum a song when I couldn't sleep. My mother taught it to me. I don't remember it anymore.* He doesn't know what to do with this. He thinks it is a non sequitur. It isn't. The reader should feel, without being told, that she has just tried to tell him something enormous and he has failed to hear it. That night she watches him sleep again and this time he does not pretend. He watches her back, through his lashes, and her face is not composed — it is wrecked, and he sees it, and he closes his eyes anyway.

**Chapter 6 — The House**
He tries to leave. Not dramatically. He tells her he's going to drive into town for groceries. He gets in the car. He drives. He comes back three hours later with nothing. He doesn't remember the drive. He remembers parking somewhere and sitting. He remembers a song on the radio that he thinks, afterwards, might have been the song she said she couldn't remember. When he comes into the kitchen she is sitting at the table and she says *you came back*, and he can't tell if it's relief or grief or something else. She says *I wasn't sure you would*. He understands, for the first time, that she has been waiting for him to not come back. That this has been a possibility she has been holding. He doesn't ask what she would have done. He goes upstairs and lies down in their bed in the afternoon light and tries to cry and can't.

**Chapter 7 — Honey**
Night. He can feel it now — not as a voice, not as a presence, but as a lightness, an ease, a willingness in his own body that isn't his. Things are easier. His hands are steadier. He knows this is bad. He goes downstairs. Maren is in the kitchen, not doing anything, just sitting. He sits across from her. He says *it was you first*. She doesn't answer. He says *you knew*. She says *I hoped*. He asks her why the honey. She says her grandmother did it, for something else, for something that didn't work, and she doesn't know why she started doing it for him, she just couldn't not. They sit a long time. He asks her, eventually, to do something. He doesn't say what. She understands. She says *I can't*. He says *please*. She says *I can't do that for you*. He says *then what*. She says *I don't know*. They go to bed. She does not watch him. She lies with her back to him and he understands this as a kind of giving up, and he is grateful for it, and ashamed of the gratitude.

**Chapter 8 — What She Did**
Morning. He wakes and she is not in the bed. He finds her in the kitchen. She has packed a bag. She tells him she is leaving. She tells him she should have left a year ago, before the house, before any of it. She tells him she doesn't know if leaving will take it with her or leave it with him or split it between them, and she doesn't know which would be worse, and she is going to find out. She is crying but her voice is steady. He realises she is not asking his permission. He realises, also, that part of him — the part that is still him — is relieved. She kisses him on the forehead like you kiss a child or a corpse. She leaves. He stands in the kitchen. The house is very quiet. He becomes aware that he is watching himself stand in the kitchen — that there is a small distance now between the watching and the standing — and that the watching is patient, and that it has all the time it needs. He thinks about the bed upstairs, still warm on her side. He thinks he might go lie down. He thinks he might not. The last line is his, and it is not the first line inverted; it is something smaller and worse.

# The Narrator — Daniel Harlow

**Background.** Thirty-four. Grew up outside Harrisburg, middle child of three, the one his mother called "the easy one" because he never made a fuss. That was the beginning of the problem, though nobody in his family would have called it a problem. He went to a small state college, studied communications, works now as a copywriter for a medical software company, remote. He is good at his job in a way that requires him to disappear into other people's voices all day, and he has come to prefer that to his own. Met Maren at twenty-six at a friend's wedding; she made fun of his tie and he was in love before the reception ended. They married fast. Were happy, he thinks, though when he tries to remember specific happy moments he finds mostly photographs and has to work backwards from those.

Something went wrong about a year and a half ago. He won't name it, even to himself. There was a stretch of months where Maren didn't get out of bed much. There was a night he slept in the other room and didn't come back for a week. There was a conversation in a car, parked outside a diner they never went into, where she said something and he said something and afterwards neither of them referred to it again. The house in the country was his idea. *A reset,* he called it. Maren agreed the way people agree to things they no longer have the energy to refuse.

**Personality and flaws.** Avoidant in a specific, practiced way. He is not cold — he is warm, in fact, and people like him — but the warmth is a skill he developed young to keep from being asked for anything harder. He apologises reflexively. He remembers everyone's birthday. He will drive two hours to help a friend move and then resent it for months without saying so. His worst quality is that he mistakes his own passivity for kindness. He thinks he is being generous when he is actually being absent. Maren used to say, early on, *you're not here, you're just nearby,* and he thought she was being cute.

He reads nonfiction. Doesn't finish books. Keeps a stack on the nightstand that Maren has stopped commenting on. Drinks two beers most nights, three if he's working late. Has not cried since his father's funeral six years ago and does not know this about himself.

**Idiosyncrasies.** Hums without noticing. Pats his pockets compulsively — phone, wallet, keys — even when sitting. Cannot throw away pens, even dead ones. Says *sorry* when he bumps into furniture. Still calls his mother every Sunday and tells her nothing.

**Physicality.** Tallish, soft in the middle now in a way that surprises him in mirrors. Brown hair going a little thin at the crown. A face people describe as *nice*, which is not the same as handsome. Moves carefully through rooms, as if worried about knocking something over. Smiles too quickly and too often. When he is thinking he touches his lower lip with his thumb.

**Motives and allegiances.** He wants, more than anything, to not have to decide. He loves Maren. He thinks he loves Maren. He is not sure anymore what the word means if he has been, as she once said, only nearby. His allegiance is to the shape of the marriage, the fact of it, rather than to her specifically — a distinction he would deny and which is nevertheless true. He wants to be a good man and has confused this with being an agreeable one.

**Voice.**

> *I told myself I was letting her sleep. That was the phrase I used, in my head, the way you use a phrase to cover a hole. I was letting her sleep. I was not avoiding her. There is a difference, I thought, and the thinking of it was the proof.*

> "I slept fine. No, really. Fine."

> *The honey was sweet and thick and I ate it every morning because she gave it to me and because not eating it would have required a conversation, and the honey was easier than the conversation, and I think this is probably the whole story of my life.*

---

# Maren Harlow (née Vos)

**Background.** Thirty-two. Only child. Her mother died when she was eleven, her father when she was twenty-four — neither death clean, both slow. She was raised in a house where women took care of things silently and then disappeared into back rooms to fall apart. Her grandmother, who helped raise her after her mother died, was a sharp woman with strange habits: rinsed coins in vinegar, wouldn't let anyone whistle indoors, kept a jar of honey by the bed and made Maren eat a spoonful when she had bad dreams. Maren stopped having the dreams eventually. Or stopped reporting them.

Something has been with her since she was a child. She would not call it possession. She would not call it anything. For a long time she thought it was a mood, a weather, the family trait on her mother's side — *the dark patch*, her grandmother called it, and fed her honey for it. It quieted when she met Daniel. For years it was almost gone. She let herself believe it had been a sickness of girlhood, grown out of. Then, about a year and a half ago, something happened between her and Daniel — a failure, a wound, something she asked him for that he did not give — and the quiet broke. She felt it wake up and she felt, to her horror, that it was not interested in her anymore. It was interested in him. In the room he had become.

She has been watching this happen for months. She has tried, in small private ways, to stop it — the honey, a song she hums some nights, standing in certain doorways longer than she needs to. These are not rituals she believes in. They are things her grandmother did, and doing them is the closest she can come to prayer.

**Personality and flaws.** Funnier than Daniel. Meaner, when she's tired. Specific in her affections and specific in her resentments. She remembers things. She is capable of not bringing something up for a year and bringing it up perfectly, on the right night, when it will do the most damage. She knows this about herself and mostly refrains and when she doesn't refrain she is not sorry. She has a low tolerance for small talk and a high tolerance for silence. She would rather say nothing than say something approximate.

She has loved Daniel with a clarity he has never matched and she has known this for a long time and it has made her lonely in a way she can't quite forgive him for. The thing inside her, when it was inside her, was almost a companion. She misses it in a way that shames her.

**Idiosyncrasies.** Hums without realising — a tune she claims not to remember. Cuts apples in a spiral, one long peel. Can't sleep with the closet door open. Reads the ends of books first. Calls Daniel *you* more often than his name, even in affection.

**Physicality.** Small, narrow, darker than Daniel — dark hair, dark eyes, olive-pale skin. Has lost weight this year without meaning to. A face that looks severe in repose and transforms entirely when she laughs, which is less often now. Moves with economy — never fidgets, never touches her hair. Stands very still when she's upset, which most people misread as calm. Her hands are always cold.

**Motives and allegiances.** She loves Daniel. She is furious with Daniel. She has been grieving him while he sits across from her at the table eating toast. Her deepest allegiance is not to him but to an older, harder thing — to not becoming her mother, who went into a back room and did not come out. She will leave before she lets that happen. She has been deciding to leave for months, and hating herself for the deciding, and staying anyway, until the decision makes itself.

**Voice.**

> "Are you."

> *He didn't hear me. I watched him not hear me and I thought, there, that's the thing, that's the shape of it, he has never heard me and something else is going to, and it already is.*

> "I used to hum a song when I couldn't sleep. My mother taught it to me. I don't remember it anymore."

> *I watched him sleep because awake he was already gone and asleep I could pretend he was only tired. That is the whole of it. I am not a good woman. I am a tired one.*

---

# The Thing

Not a character in the conventional sense, and I won't write it as one. But worth anchoring, for my own use.

It is not a demon. It has no name, no origin story, no rules. It is a hunger that prefers certain shapes of people — the ones with room in them, the ones who have practiced not being there. It moved through Maren's family for at least three generations, possibly more; nobody wrote it down. It does not speak. It does not announce itself. What it does is make things easier. The hand stops shaking. The sentence comes smoothly. The smile arrives without being summoned. Its gift is ease, and ease is what it takes first and what it leaves last.

It does not want Maren anymore. She fought it too long and got too thin around it. Daniel is softer. Daniel has been practicing for it his whole life.

It will not be defeated in this story. The question is only who carries it, and at what cost, and whether carrying is the same as being carried.

# Chapter 1 — Vigil

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping.

I had trained myself, by then, in the shape of a sleeping man. The mouth a little open. The breath slow and even through the nose. One hand loose on the pillow, the other tucked somewhere under the blanket, as if forgotten there. It was easier than I would have guessed. You only have to hold very still and let your face go.

The room was dark but not completely. There was a moon somewhere doing moon things through the curtain, and the alarm clock by her side of the bed put a small red weather of light on the ceiling. I could see her without seeming to. She was sitting up. She had pushed the covers down to her waist. She was not moving. She was looking at me with the kind of attention you bring to a thing you are trying to memorise, or to a thing you are trying to forgive.

This was the fifth time. Maybe the sixth. I had stopped trusting the count.

The first time I had woken by accident, turned, seen her, and said her name, and she had startled and laughed and said she couldn't sleep, and I had believed her, or I had decided to believe her, which is the same thing if you do it fast enough. The second time I had not said anything. I had closed my eyes and listened to her breathing until eventually the mattress shifted and she lay down again and I heard her breath slow and even out, though I could not tell, then or now, whether she was actually asleep or only performing it back at me.

By the fifth time it was a routine. She watched. I pretended. We took turns being the one who did not know.

I counted in my head. I had read somewhere that you could slow your heart by counting your breaths and I was not trying to slow my heart, I was trying to keep it steady, to not let it do the thing it wanted to do, which was to clatter up into my throat and give me away. One. Two. Three. The mattress did not move. Four. Five. Six. Still nothing. Seven. Eight. I could feel her looking. It was a pressure on the side of my face. I have never understood people who say they cannot feel when someone is watching them; I have always felt it, even as a child, even across rooms.

At fourteen I tilted my head, very slightly, as if turning in sleep, and I opened my eyes to slits, and I looked at her through the mesh of my own lashes.

Her face, in that half-light, was not the face she wore in the day. I don't mean it was the wrong face. I mean it was a face I had not been allowed to see. Her mouth was not set. Her eyes were not sharp. She looked, I thought, like someone watching a house burn down from across a field. Not running toward it. Not running away. Just watching, because there was nothing else to do and because it had been her house.

I closed my eyes.

I lay there a long time and counted and kept my breathing slow and did not think, or tried not to think, because the thinking was the thing that would give me away. Eventually she lay down. She did it carefully, the way she did everything now, as if the bed were a thing that might wake. She turned onto her side, away from me. After a while her breath lengthened and I could not tell if she was asleep. I could never tell anymore. We had become very good, the two of us, at faking it for each other.

I watched the ceiling go from black to grey. I watched the red light of the clock become less important as the window became more important. When it was light enough to call morning I got up and went downstairs in my socks and stood at the kitchen sink and drank a glass of water and looked out at the yard, which was full of the kind of fog that sits on low grass and makes you feel underwater. The house made its small morning sounds. I didn't turn the kettle on. I didn't want the noise.

After a while I heard her on the stairs.

"You're up early," she said.

"Couldn't sleep," I said, which was true and a lie at once, the way most of what I said to her now was true and a lie at once.

"Mm," she said. She came and stood next to me at the sink and looked out at the same fog. She did not touch me. We had stopped touching without deciding to; it had happened the way a lamp stops working, some filament somewhere, and neither of us had been willing to be the one to say the lamp is broken. She smelled like sleep and a little like the soap she used, which was her grandmother's soap, some brand you could only get by mail. Her hair was down. Her feet were bare. She was very small next to me, as she had always been, and I had always been a little surprised by it, and this morning I was surprised by it again, and then I was surprised that I was still capable of being surprised by her.

"Did you sleep?" she said.

"Yeah," I said. "Fine."

She nodded. She did not look at me. She was looking at the fog.

"Good," she said. "I'm glad."

And the terrible thing — the thing I could not get past, standing there at the sink with the cold glass in my hand — was that I believed her. She was glad. Whatever else was wrong, that part was true.

# Chapter 2 — The Honey

She kept the honey on the counter in a small jar with no label. It was darker than the honey you buy in stores, almost brown, and thicker, and it smelled like something more than honey — a little like smoke, a little like the inside of a drawer. She had it sent from somewhere. I had never asked where. I had never asked anything about it. This was, I understood now, the same as lying.

She put the spoon in front of me next to the coffee. She did this every morning. She had done it every morning for — I tried to count and couldn't. Months. Since the house. Before the house, maybe. I could not remember when she had started, which was its own kind of answer.

"Eat your honey," she said.

"I know."

"I'm just saying."

I ate the honey. It coated the roof of my mouth and stayed there a long time after. I drank the coffee on top of it and the coffee tasted strange, as it always did after the honey, sweet and a little metallic, like I had been sucking a coin.

"Thanks," I said.

"Mm."

She was already moving toward the door, a jacket half on, a pair of gardening gloves in her back pocket. She did something with the garden every morning that I did not understand. There was not much garden. There was a vegetable patch she had dug in the spring, which had produced three tomatoes and a lot of disappointment, and a border of things I could not name along the fence. She would go out there and crouch and put her hands into the dirt and stay like that for a long time. Once I had watched her from the window and she had not moved for almost an hour. I had told myself she was thinking.

"I'll be out back," she said.

"Okay."

She left. The door clicked shut with its particular click, the one I had learned to listen for. The house without her in it was a different house. Quieter in the wrong way. You could feel the rooms she wasn't in.

I opened the laptop. I had a deadline. Patient-facing copy for a scheduling platform — the kind of writing where you have to pretend that going to the doctor is a thing people want to do. *Your health, on your time.* I had written that line, or one very like it, probably twenty times in my career. It came out of me the way water comes out of a tap.

I worked. Or I sat in front of the screen and the screen received me. After a while I realised my hand was resting on the same page of my notebook and I did not know for how long. I looked at the clock. It was 10:40. I remembered sitting down at 9:15. I remembered the first paragraph. I did not remember the hour and a half in between.

I got up. I walked a circle around the kitchen table, which is the kind of thing I do when I don't want to notice what I've just noticed. I poured more coffee. I drank it standing.

"I'm going," she said.

"Okay."

"I should have gone a year ago."

"Okay."

"Before the house. Before any of this."

"Okay, Mar."

She nodded. She did not cry. Her voice was steady in the way a voice is steady when a person has used up the part of themselves that cries.

"I don't know what it does," she said. "If I leave. I don't know if it comes with me. I don't know if it stays with you. I don't know if it — if it splits. I don't know. It might do any of those. I don't know which would be worse. I've been thinking about it for a long time and I don't know."

"Okay."

"I'm going to find out."

"Okay."

"I'm sorry, Daniel."

"It's okay."

"It isn't."

"No," I said. "It isn't. But you can say it. You can say it's okay. I'll say it back. It's okay."

She looked at me a long time. She was looking for something in my face. I don't know what she was looking for. I don't know if she found it. Something in her eased, a little, and she nodded once, small.

"Okay," she said.

I stood in the doorway. I did not go to her. I had the thought that I could — that I could cross the kitchen and kneel by her chair and put my face in her lap and ask her not to. I had the thought clearly. I watched myself have it. And I watched the part of me that was still me consider it, and I watched the other part, the easier part, the part with the steady hands, consider it too, and I understood that I could not tell, anymore, which of them wanted it more. Which of them would use it.

I stayed in the doorway.

She stood up. She put her coat on. She picked up the keys. She picked up the bag. She came across the kitchen toward me and I thought for a second she was going to go around me, out the door, without — and then she stopped in front of me and she put her hand up and cupped the side of my face.

Her hand was very cold.

She looked at me, and she did the thing she used to do a long time ago when we were first married, which was to look at me as if she were taking my picture — holding the look a beat longer than was comfortable, making a record of it. She had not done this in years. I had forgotten she used to do it. I remembered, now, standing in the kitchen doorway with her palm cold on my cheek, that she had used to do it every time she left the house.

She leaned up and kissed me on the forehead.

It was the kiss you give a child. It was the kiss you give a body at a wake. It was both at once and she knew it and she did it anyway, and then she took her hand down, and she went past me into the hall, and I heard the front door, and I heard the car, and I heard the car go down the drive, and I heard it get smaller, and I heard it gone.

I stood in the doorway of the kitchen.

The house was quiet. The fridge ran. The radiator ticked. A bird did something in the eaves and stopped. I was aware, in a distant calm way, that I should be feeling something, and I was not feeling it, or I was feeling it at a remove, as if through a wall. I noticed this. I noticed, too, that I was noticing — that there was a small gap now between me and the noticing, a thin clear space, and the space was watching. The space was patient. The space had all the time it needed.

I thought about going upstairs. The bed would still be warm on her side. I could lie down in the warm place and put my face in the pillow and breathe her in, which would be the thing a man would do, the thing I would have done, a year ago, a week ago, yesterday. I thought about doing it. I did not move.

The honey jar was on the counter where she always left it. The spoon was beside it. She had set them out before she went. She had done it without telling me. She had done it the way she had been doing it every morning for a long time now, which was without deciding, which was because she could not not do it. I looked at the jar. I looked at the spoon.

After a while I went and I ate the honey.

It was sweet. It stayed in the roof of my mouth.

I stood at the counter with the empty spoon in my hand and I thought: *she left it for me. She left it and she went.* And I thought: *I ate it.* And I did not know, standing there, which of us had done the eating.

I put the spoon in the sink. I ran the water over it. I watched my hand, which did not shake, and which went on not shaking, and I stood at the sink a long time after the spoon was clean.

The plan's note that "I can't do that for you" should be said "the way you say a thing you have been saying to yourself for a long time in preparation for saying it out loud" is executed almost verbatim, and it works.

**What Doesn't Quite Land**

The phrase "like weather you have been watching come in across a field" is slightly generic as a simile — it's competent but not distinctive. The chapter's ending, with the "warm stone" of gratitude, is effective but the "warm stone" image is perhaps the one moment where the prose reaches for something slightly more literary than it needs to. It works, but it's the chapter's most visible seam.

The observation "the fact that I had not asked was the whole shape of our marriage, was the exact shape" is a moment of tell-don't-show — Daniel articulating the thematic meaning of his own passivity too cleanly. The story has already shown this; the narrator doesn't need to name it so explicitly.

**Overall Assessment**

This is a strong chapter — controlled, emotionally intelligent, faithful to its characters and its plan. The horror is genuinely present in the ease Daniel feels, in Maren's exhausted love, in the honey ritual that may or may not have done anything. The chapter earns its darkness. It is not a masterpiece — there are small moments of over-articulation and one or two generic images — but it is accomplished, serious work.

[Analysis]

This is a genuinely accomplished piece of horror writing that earns most of what it reaches for. Let me work through it carefully.

The chapter opens with a classic but well-executed beat — the cold side of the bed — and moves into the kitchen scene with real economy. The staging is precise: the keys on the table, her hand next to them rather than on them. That detail is excellent. It communicates her ambivalence without announcing it, and it's the kind of specific, observed detail that separates competent writing from good writing.

The dialogue is the chapter's most distinctive formal choice and its most successful gambit. Daniel's repeated "Okay" functions as a kind of dissociation made audible — he is present enough to respond and absent enough that the response is always the same. This is consistent with his character profile (avoidant, passive, mistaking absence for kindness) and it creates genuine unease. When Maren says "It isn't" and he agrees — "No. It isn't. But you can say it" — there's a moment of real intimacy and real horror simultaneously. He is coaching her through a lie they both need. This is sophisticated.

The passage where Daniel considers going to her — kneeling by her chair, putting his face in her lap — and then watches himself consider it, and then watches "the other part, the easier part, the part with the steady hands" consider it too, is the chapter's best moment. It executes the possession concept without any of the genre's usual furniture. The horror is in the epistemological problem: he cannot tell which part of him wants what. This is exactly what the plan promised and it delivers.

The forehead kiss is handled well. The narration earns the double reading (child/corpse) by not overexplaining it — "It was both at once and she knew it and she did it anyway" is the right amount of acknowledgment. The detail of her old habit of looking at him as if taking his picture, which she used to do every time she left the house, is quietly devastating and feels genuinely discovered rather than planted.

The honey ending is the chapter's most deliberate structural choice and it mostly works. The ambiguity — "I did not know, standing there, which of us had done the eating" — is earned because the honey has been established across the story as Maren's protective gesture, her grandmother's remedy. Her leaving it out before she goes is a final act of love that is also, possibly, futile. The narrator eating it anyway, and not knowing if it's him or the thing eating it, closes the loop without closing the story. The final image — watching his hand not shake, standing at the sink long after the spoon is clean — is appropriately bleak and restrained.

Where the chapter is slightly less successful: the repetition of "Okay" is effective but risks becoming a tic. By the fifth or sixth instance, a reader might feel the technique rather than the emotion. The plan called for the ending to be "smaller and worse" than an inversion of the opening, and it achieves this, but the final line ("I stood at the sink a long time after the spoon was clean") is perhaps a touch too composed — it's a good sentence but it's a literary sentence, and the plan explicitly said "not reaching for the literary register; letting it arrive only when earned." This is a minor complaint; the sentence does earn it.

The chapter follows its plan with impressive fidelity. Maren packs a bag, tells him she doesn't know what leaving will do, kisses him on the forehead "like you kiss a child or a corpse," and leaves. He becomes aware of the watching distance between himself and himself. He thinks about the bed. The honey is the final beat. Every element from the plan is present and most are executed better than the plan described them.

Character consistency is strong. Daniel's "Okay" repetition is perfectly him — the man who apologizes to furniture, who says "sorry" reflexively, who has practiced not being there. Maren's steadiness, her cold hands, her economy of movement, her final act of leaving the honey — all consistent. The detail of her looking at him as if taking his picture, established in the character profile as something she used to do when leaving the house, is a beautiful callback that feels organic rather than planted.

The dialogue is sparse and evasive as planned, and it works. "Are you going to be okay?" is never asked. "I love you" is never said. The absence of those phrases is louder than their presence would be.

One small weakness: the line "Her voice was steady in the way a voice is steady when a person has used up the part of themselves that cries" is slightly over-explained. The chapter has been showing us this; it doesn't need to tell us the mechanism.

Overall this is a high-quality chapter that executes a difficult tonal and conceptual task with considerable skill. The possession horror is entirely psychological and entirely convincing. The relationship horror is real. The ending is genuinely uncomfortable without being sensational.

writing_prompt.title: Babysitter's Payback
writing_prompt.writing_prompt:
Pulp Revenge Tale
Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: They fucked with the wrong babysitter.

step_outputs.1:
# Brainstorming

**Initial Prompt Interpretation**
"They fucked with the wrong babysitter" — pure pulp. Think Grindhouse, Tarantino, early Rodriguez, the babysitter-as-avenger subgenre. The phrase promises genre violence, dark humor, a protagonist whose appearance belies their capability. The babysitter is underestimated — that's the core irony that powers pulp revenge.

**Character ideas for the babysitter:**
- Ex-cartel enforcer trying to live quiet life, hiding out in suburbia
- Former child soldier turned nursing student
- Ex-Mossad agent in witness protection
- A retired assassin, now 50s, taking side gigs
- A teenage girl who's secretly something else — reformed serial killer, witch, revenant
- A trans woman who was a Marine Recon sniper
- Nun who left the church after doing "wet work" for the Vatican
- A quiet 19-year-old whose father was a hitman and taught her everything
- Someone hiding from a past gang; the past comes knocking

I like the 19-year-old angle best — it maps to the "babysitter" role believably. Or late 20s grad student vibe.

**The kids:**
- One kid, a precocious 8-year-old boy who becomes her partner-in-survival
- Two kids — older girl and little brother
- A single child with a medical condition (gives stakes/tension)
- Kids of a wealthy family — maybe the parents are the reason trouble comes
- Kids whose father is a crooked DA, judge, mob accountant

**The antagonists:**
- Home invasion crew — wrong house, actually there for something specific
- Kidnappers targeting the kids for ransom
- Hitmen who found her cover identity
- Local meth gang who doesn't know what they walked into
- Dirty cops
- A cult

**Setting:**
- Isolated lake house in winter
- Suburban McMansion
- Desert compound
- Small Texas town
- Rainy Pacific Northwest
- New Mexico, monsoon season

I like isolated + one night, classic unity of place and time.

**Plot structures (8 chapters, ~1000 words each = 8k words total):**

*Version A: Hidden Past*
Ch 1: Setup — babysitter arrives, meets kids, establishes normalcy, hints of her past
Ch 2: Intruders arrive, situation escalates fast
Ch 3: First kill, she surprises them, kids hidden
Ch 4: Cat and mouse through house
Ch 5: She's hurt, captured or cornered, reveals more backstory
Ch 6: Turns tables, hunts them
Ch 7: Confrontation with the boss — reveals why they came
Ch 8: Aftermath, new normal, dark coda

*Version B: The Parents Did It*
Parents are involved in something bad, babysitter uncovers it while protecting kids.

*Version C: Revenge Proper*
They hurt one of the kids first — now it's revenge not defense.

**Tone:**
- Pulpy but not cartoonish
- Sharp prose, punchy chapters
- Some dark humor, some genuine menace
- Tarantino-esque dialogue mixed with Cormac-lite violence
- Could lean toward Jack Ketchum/Gillian Flynn in its meanness

**Possible title beats / chapter titles:**
- "The House on Marigold Lane"
- "Rules of the House"
- "Broken Window"
- "The First One Down"
- "What She Was Before"
- "Basement Work"
- "Meet the Boss"
- "Morning"

**Specific ideas I'm excited about:**
- Babysitter has a tattoo she hides; kids notice it
- She established three rules at the start that pay off later
- A Chekhov item introduced innocuously (knitting needles, a hair pin, nail file)
- The kid becomes her accomplice in a small, unsettling way — takes agency
- One villain underestimates her right up to the last second
- A phone call to someone from her past for "cleanup"
- Final image: her baking cookies with the kids the next morning, casual, a bandage somewhere

**Name ideas:**
- Babysitter: Jules, Cora, Mira, Rook, Sadie, Wren
- Kids: Eli and Maddie; or just Sam; Theo
- Villain: Dutch, Marco, someone with a title like "The Preacher"

# Reflection

The prompt is inherently pulp, so leaning into genre feels right. The challenge with 8k words is pacing — I need to resist front-loading backstory and instead earn revelation through action. The phrase "fucked with the wrong babysitter" is a punchline; the story is the setup to that punchline.

What works:
- The single-night, single-location structure has built-in momentum and forces every chapter to advance
- A young-looking protagonist with a hidden lethal past is the most genre-satisfying version; it creates immediate irony
- Two kids (older sister, younger brother) lets me have one who's perceptive and one who provides vulnerability/stakes. Or just one kid for tighter focus.
- Home invasion that's at the *wrong* house feels fresh and plays directly with the prompt — the antagonists literally fucked with the wrong one
- Alternatively: antagonists at the *right* house (coming for her, or for something the parents have) creates a deeper mystery

What doesn't work as well:
- Too much backstory exposition will kill pace; I need to show her competence more than explain it
- Making her a former government spook feels overdone; something messier is more interesting — cartel enforcer's daughter, or she was the one hired when hitmen needed hitmen
- Supernatural angle (witch, revenant) could be fun but might dilute the grounded pulp feel
- A cult would require too much setup for 8k words
- Overly comedic tone could undercut the "revenge" element — I want menace with flecks of humor, not parody

On protagonist: I think a woman in her early 20s, quiet, polite, hiding in plain sight. Maybe she grew up in a criminal family and got out, or did something terrible young and is atoning. Her competence should feel earned, not superhero-ish. She should get hurt, be scared, make mistakes.

On antagonists: Three or four works best for pacing. A crew with distinct personalities — the leader who's smart, the brute, the loose cannon, the reluctant one. Classic but effective in 8k.

On the twist/reveal: Best if the reason they came isn't random — it connects to either the parents' secret OR the babysitter's past. The latter is more satisfying for the prompt: they came for her, thinking she'd be easy. They were wrong. That IS the prompt, literalized.

Pacing across 8 chapters: I want Ch 1 to be deceptively gentle and domestic, Ch 2 to shift the air, Ch 3 to deliver first violence. Middle chapters (4-6) should be the hunt and reversal. Ch 7 is climax/confrontation with the boss who must know her. Ch 8 is the morning after — cookies, kids, police not called, someone gets buried. A dark coda that recontextualizes her.

Tone target: Noir-pulp with a cold, spare voice. Short sentences. Dialogue that bites. Violence that's ugly, not cool. A protagonist we root for despite — because of — her darkness. Think *You Were Never Really Here* meets *The Babysitter* meets a Jordan Harper short story.

I'm drawn to the version where the crew is after her specifically — her past caught up. The parents being out at some benefit gala, the kids sleeping upstairs, and four men showing up to collect a debt. She has to protect the kids, yes, but she also has to become what she was again — and we watch her decide she's okay with that. That's the juiciest thematic meat.
step_outputs.2:
# Intention

I'm writing a pulp revenge story that takes its prompt seriously as both premise and punchline. The phrase "they fucked with the wrong babysitter" is the shape the whole piece pours into: a setup of deceptive domesticity, a collision with violence, and a protagonist whose competence is the grim joke that pays off the title.

**Protagonist:** A young woman in her early twenties — I'll call her Wren — who grew up inside a criminal world and got out. She babysits for a suburban family in a quiet town because it's the opposite of what she was. The men who come for her tonight are from her past. The kids are incidental to their plan but central to hers.

**Antagonists:** A crew of four, distinct: a cold leader who knows who she was, a brute, a jumpy young one, and a reluctant middle-aged wheelman. This lets me vary the kills and the tension, and gives me someone whose fear foreshadows her capability.

**Structure:** Single night, single house (with brief spillover to the yard/garage). Unity of time and place, classic pulp containment. Eight chapters of ~1000 words, each a clear beat. I want the first chapter to feel almost like a different genre — domestic, warm, slightly melancholy — so the turn lands harder.

**Voice & style:** Close third on Wren. Short sentences. Spare, noir-adjacent prose with a cold undercurrent. Dialogue that cuts. Violence that's ugly and physical — not balletic, not cool. Some dark, dry humor, but no winking. I want the reader to feel the weight of what she's capable of, not cheer it like a video game.

**What I'm aiming for:**
- Earned menace through action and small specifics, not backstory monologues
- A protagonist whose darkness is real — she's not purely heroic, she's efficient, and that's unsettling
- Kids who feel like actual children: scared, clever, a little weird
- A reveal (the boss knows her) that reframes the fight as personal
- A morning-after coda that's almost tender, almost sweet, and completely wrong

**What I'm avoiding:**
- Long flashback exposition dumps; backstory in drips, through objects and dialogue
- Supernatural elements
- Parody tone or quippy action-movie banter
- Making her invincible; she gets hurt, scared, and makes at least one mistake that costs
- Redemption arc cliché — she doesn't need to be saved, and she doesn't quite get saved here

**Key motifs/objects to seed early and pay off:**
- A set of three "house rules" Wren tells the kids (paid off in reversal)
- Knitting she brings along (needles later used; the half-finished scarf as image)
- A phone number memorized, never dialed in years — used at the end for cleanup
- A tattoo on her ribs the little girl glimpses
- Chocolate chip cookies prepped in Ch 1, baked in Ch 8

# Chapter Planning

**Chapter 1 — Rules of the House (~1000 words)**
Wren arrives at the Mercers' house on a Friday night. The parents — a lawyer and his wife — are going to a charity gala. Two kids: Maddie, nine, sharp-eyed; Eli, six, clinging. Establish the suburban calm, the big house, the woods behind it. Wren is polite, quiet, mid-twenties, knits, brings her own bag. She lays out three rules for the kids: *don't open the door for anyone, stay upstairs if I say so, and if I tell you to run, you run and don't look back.* Maddie notices a tattoo on Wren's ribs when she reaches up. They bake cookies, read a book. Parents call in. A car slows on the street outside; Wren notices. End on her locking the back door twice.

**Chapter 2 — Headlights (~1000 words)**
Kids are in bed. Wren knits in the living room, TV low, but her attention is on the windows. A black SUV parks two houses down. Four men get out. She watches for thirty seconds, then moves — wakes Maddie, not Eli. Tells Maddie to take her brother to the attic crawlspace, lock it, and not come out no matter what she hears. Maddie asks why. Wren says, "Because I told you to run." Wren goes downstairs, phone in hand. She doesn't call 911. She dials a memorized number, leaves a clipped message, and hangs up. The doorbell rings. She opens a drawer in the kitchen. End on her walking toward the door.

**Chapter 3 — First One Down (~1000 words)**
She doesn't answer the door. The men try the handle, then go around. A window breaks at the back. Wren is already in the mudroom. The jumpy young one (Denny) comes through first — she takes him with a meat mallet and a kitchen knife, fast and ugly, before he can shout. He dies noisy anyway, and she knows the others heard. She drags him behind the island. The brute (Marco) calls his name; no answer. The leader's voice — calm, familiar — says, "Wren. Come on." She freezes at her own name. So they know. End on her recognizing something in that voice.

**Chapter 4 — What She Was Before (~1000 words)**
Cat and mouse in the dark house. Wren cuts the breakers. She moves room to room, using the geography she's memorized. A flashback in flickers only: a man teaching her to hold a knife at thirteen, her walking out of a house at nineteen with blood on her shoes, a number written on the inside of a matchbook. She takes the brute next in the laundry room — a bad, grappling kill, and she gets cut badly across the forearm. She binds it with a dishtowel. The reluctant wheelman (Ray) is in the hall calling her name too, saying he didn't want this, he was just driving. She almost believes him. Almost. End with her upstairs, bleeding, listening to Eli cry faintly through the attic floor.

**Chapter 5 — The Wheelman (~1000 words)**
Ray finds her — or thinks he does. They talk through a wall. He tells her the boss is Holloway — and the name lands. Holloway was the man she left for dead four years ago. He survived. He's been looking for her ever since. Ray says he has a daughter, he just wants to walk out. Wren listens. She lets him think he's convinced her. When he comes around the corner with his hands half-raised, she kills him with the knitting needles — clean, through the throat. She sits beside his body a moment. This one she feels. The kids are still crying above her. She wipes her face and goes to find Holloway.

**Chapter 6 — Basement Work (~1000 words)**
Holloway is patient; he's waited four years. He's in the basement, where he went down to cut the phones — not realizing she'd already cut them from the attic wiring she knows this house because she's babysat here fifty times. He expects her to come from the stairs. She comes from the bulkhead. It goes wrong — he's faster than she remembered, older and meaner. He gets her down. He talks while he hurts her: about the man she killed, about what he taught her, about how she was the best thing he ever made. She lets him talk. Her hand finds the box cutter in her back pocket. End on a short, decisive motion and the wet sound that follows.

**Chapter 7 — Morning Will Come (~1000 words)**
Holloway is alive, barely, zip-tied to a pipe. She doesn't kill him yet. She climbs the stairs, her arm in ribbons, and calls up to Maddie in the attic. The girl opens the hatch, Eli behind her. Wren tells them everything is okay now, that some bad men came to the wrong house, and she made them leave. Maddie looks at the blood on her shirt and says nothing. Wren cleans up what she can, puts the kids in her own bed, sits outside the door. The number she called in Ch 2 calls back: a woman's voice, asking for an address. She gives it. Two hours until dawn. She goes back down to Holloway. They talk, quietly, for the last time. She finishes it before the sun comes up.

**Chapter 8 — Cookies (~1000 words)**
Dawn. A plain van with no plates. Two women in coveralls who do not speak to her beyond necessities. The house is cleaned in ninety minutes — a thoroughness that should frighten anyone who sees it. Wren showers, changes into clothes from her bag, bandages her arm beneath a long-sleeved henley. She bakes the cookies she and Eli mixed the night before. When Maddie comes down, Wren pours her orange juice. Maddie asks, quiet: *Were you always a babysitter?* Wren says: *No. But I am now.* The parents come home at nine, flushed from champagne and a late breakfast, apologizing. Eli runs to his mother. Maddie looks at Wren a long time. Wren smiles. She gets paid in cash. She walks out past the neighbor watering his lawn and nods good morning. End image: her on a bus, scarf half-knit in her lap, picking up a stitch she dropped in the dark last night.
step_outputs.3:
# How a Human Writer Might Approach This

A human writer tackling "they fucked with the wrong babysitter" would probably start with *attitude*. The prompt is a brag, a tagline, a bumper sticker of a sentence. It has swagger. A human writer would decide early how to relate to that swagger: embrace it fully (go lurid, go bloody, go fun), ironize it (make the "revenge" feel hollow), or undercut it (make the violence genuinely sickening). The worst move is to do all three at once tentatively — which is exactly what an LLM tends to do, hedging its bets.

A human would probably also write from some specific seed: a real babysitting gig they remember, a woman they knew who seemed too calm, a house they've been in. Something grounding. They'd bring weird specific details — the smell of a particular brand of cookie dough, the way a specific kind of screen door sounds, a song stuck in someone's head. These idiosyncrasies are what make prose feel lived-in rather than assembled.

A human might also write messier. They'd leave threads hanging. They'd give a character a weird quirk that isn't "justified" by plot. They might start a chapter in the middle of a thought. They'd trust the reader to catch up. They'd let a scene go longer than it "should" if the texture was interesting, or clip a scene brutally short if the point had been made.

Crucially, a human writer doing pulp knows pulp has *meanness* and *appetite* in it. It's not polite. It doesn't apologize. It's okay with being ugly, with being unfair, with leaving a bad taste. An LLM almost always wants to be liked.

# General LLM Failings That Would Hurt This Piece

**1. The Safety Reflex.** LLMs soften violence, soften language, soften moral ambiguity. They'll describe a stabbing in metaphor rather than physicality. They'll have characters feel bad in ways that editorialize the reader's response. For a pulp revenge tale, this is death. The violence needs to be ugly and specific. The protagonist needs to be allowed to be cold without the prose apologizing for her.

**2. The Redemption Reflex / Bow-Tying.** LLMs love neat endings. They love a moral. They love growth arcs. Pulp revenge doesn't want this. The ending should leave residue. The "morning after cookies" scene I planned is good, but I can see the LLM version of it — where Maddie's question becomes a tidy emotional beat and Wren has a moment of quiet self-knowledge. That would ruin it. It should be *strange*, not resolved.

**3. Impressive-Sounding Prose.** LLMs reach for the cinematic, the operatic, the weighty sentence. "The night pressed in like a held breath." "Violence had always been her native tongue." This kind of thing is a tell. Good pulp prose is often boring on the sentence level — it's about image, rhythm, and restraint, not ornate metaphor. Overwriting kills pulp dead.

**4. Over-Explanation.** LLMs explain what a character is feeling, then describe how they show it, then have another character notice it. Triple redundancy. A human trusts one of those three to do the job.

**5. Symmetry and Symbol-Stacking.** LLMs love to tie motifs together too tightly — the tattoo, the knitting, the three rules, the cookies, the phone number — each paid off with a satisfying click. I've already planned five motifs that all get paid off neatly. That's too many clicks. Real writing leaves some motifs unresolved or lets them just be texture.

**6. Generic Character Voices.** LLMs make tough guys sound like tough guys from movies. They speak in lines, not dialogue. "Come on, Wren." "Don't make this harder than it has to be." A human would make at least one of these men speak weirdly, off-model, memorably.

**7. Pacing Evenness.** LLMs spread action evenly across planned beats. Humans let scenes breathe or strangle. A fight might take a paragraph; a silence might take a page.

**8. The Competent Woman Archetype.** This is a specific LLM trap — the Cool Assassin Lady who is calm, measured, efficient, and makes grim one-liners. She's a Pinterest board. A real character would have a tic, a fear, an irrational behavior, a weakness that isn't plot-relevant.

**9. Sanitized Interiority.** LLMs give protagonists thoughts that are morally presentable. Wren would probably have at least one thought in this story that is genuinely ugly — enjoyment, contempt, cruelty — and an LLM would flinch from writing it.

**10. Ending Benediction.** LLMs almost can't help closing on a resonant, slightly poetic image that gestures at theme. My "picking up a stitch she dropped in the dark last night" ending is… exactly that. It's a tell.

# Deep Dive Critique of the Plan

**The Protagonist is Too Clean.**
Wren as planned is a genre type — the quiet lethal woman who got out and has rules. I gave her knitting (cozy), a tattoo (mysterious), and a hidden past (tropey). She needs something that doesn't fit — a mean streak the book doesn't excuse, a pettiness, a weird fixation, a specific bad habit. Does she steal small things from the houses she sits at? Does she hate one of the kids a little? Does she have a crush on the dad she doesn't act on but notices in herself with disgust? Something human and unflattering.

**The Kids are Furniture.**
Maddie "perceptive" and Eli "little and scared" — these are placeholders. They have no texture. Real kids are weirder. Eli should have an obsession (a specific toy, a specific word). Maddie should have a thing she's lying about. They should be annoying in places, not just endangered.

**The Crew is a Checklist.**
Cold leader, brute, jumpy one, reluctant wheelman — this is literally the Four Guys of pulp cliché. At least one of them needs to surprise me. Maybe the brute isn't a brute — he's quiet and sad. Maybe the jumpy young one is the most competent. Maybe the leader isn't the scariest.

**The Plot is Too Neat.**
Each chapter has its designated kill, its designated reveal. Ch 3 kill #1, Ch 4 kill #2, Ch 5 kill #3, Ch 6 the boss. This is videogame structure. Human writing would break this rhythm — maybe two kills happen fast and close, maybe one kill happens offstage, maybe she tries to kill someone and fails, maybe the order gets confused, maybe one of them just runs away and lives.

**The Backstory is Too Legible.**
"Holloway is the man she left for dead four years ago" — this is a mechanical reveal. It clicks into place. Better if her history is murkier, partially withheld even from the ending. The reader should feel the weight of it without getting the full account.

**The Motifs are Over-Engineered.**
Three rules, tattoo, knitting, phone number, cookies, scarf, matchbook — I'm stacking Chekhov's items. A human writer would seed two, max, and let them do heavy lifting. Some of these need to just be texture, or disappear.

**The Ending is Too Graceful.**
The cookies scene is strong conceptually but I've written it too nicely in the plan. The cleanup crew arriving, the bandaged arm, the cash payment, the bus, the scarf — it's all coherent and symbolic. A human would disrupt this. Maybe she's still bleeding through the shirt. Maybe Eli says something awful and funny. Maybe she doesn't take the bus, she just walks. Maybe the neighbor is suspicious. Maybe she forgets something at the house.

**Dialogue Beats are Movie-Dialogue.**
"Because I told you to run." "Come on, Wren." "I just want to walk out." These are all fine, and all from the LLM dialogue handbook. At least some lines need to be off-rhythm, accidental, even dumb.

**The Moral Temperature is Too Stable.**
Wren is sympathetic throughout. The plan never really asks the reader to be disturbed by her. For the piece to have teeth, there should be at least one moment where we recoil — not at the violence, but at her.

**Chapter 6 (Holloway monologues while hurting her) is Classic Villain Monologue.**
This is the most LLM thing in the plan. Villains explaining themselves to captive heroes is pulp, yes, but the specific texture I've planned — "about how she was the best thing he ever made" — is generic. It should be more specific, weirder, or cut entirely.

**The Cleanup Crew is Too Cool.**
Two women in coveralls, ninety minutes, efficient. This is a setpiece from *Pulp Fiction* / *Mr. & Mrs. Smith* / every show with a fixer. It's the lazy choice. If I keep it, it needs to be weirder — older women, maybe one is chatty, maybe they don't come and she has to do it herself, maybe only one comes and she's scared of Wren.

# Ideas to Make it More Human

- Give Wren a specific, unflattering detail: she's been skimming hours on her timecard at another job, or she's sleeping with someone married, or she genuinely dislikes one of the kids she's sat for (not these ones, but she's thought it about kids before).
- Let one of the men live. Not as a mercy — as a problem. Loose ends.
- Don't reveal all the backstory. Let Holloway call her a name that isn't Wren and leave that hanging.
- Make one kill go *badly* in a non-cool way — she throws up, or her hand won't stop shaking, or she kills the wrong person (a neighbor who came to check on a noise — this would be devastating and real).
- Cut at least one motif. Pick the two strongest and drop the rest, or demote them to background.
- Write at least one paragraph that is deliberately flat, almost reportorial, as contrast to more charged prose.
- Let a chapter open mid-action without orientation.
- Give Eli a specific toy he keeps talking about. Let that toy be the last thing seen, not some grand symbolic image.
- Let Maddie be actively unhelpful at a key moment — panic, make noise, do the wrong thing. Kids do that.
- Have Wren make a real mistake with consequences, not just "get hurt" as a cost of combat.
- Let the ending be anticlimactic in some specific way. She doesn't get on a bus to new adventures. She goes back to her shitty apartment and the dishes are still in the sink from yesterday.
- Allow ugliness in her interiority — a thought about one of the kids that's uncharitable, a flash of enjoyment during a kill, boredom during the boss's speech.
- Let the prose be ruder. Let it swear. Let it be sour.
- Consider first person for one chapter, or a letter, or some disruption to close-third uniformity. Maybe not — but consider it.
- Don't make her competence feel like a superpower. Make it feel like a disease.

# Intention

This is a pulp revenge story and I'm going to let it be one — bloody, mean, with appetite. The prompt is a brag and I'm going to earn the brag, but I'm going to resist the LLM instinct to make the protagonist admirable, the violence stylish, or the ending resonant-in-a-poetic-way. I want the reader to finish the story a little unsettled by how much they rooted for her.

**Protagonist.** Wren, early twenties, was raised inside something bad and got most of the way out. She babysits because it pays cash and nobody asks questions and because she likes kids better than adults most days. She is not a Cool Assassin Woman. She's tired. Her apartment is a mess. She has a specific unflattering habit — she reads the parents' medicine cabinets, sometimes takes a pill, sometimes pockets a twenty off a dresser if it's loose. Small thefts. She's aware this is petty and does it anyway. During the violence, she will feel things we're not supposed to admit characters feel: focus that edges into pleasure, boredom during a monologue, a flash of contempt for someone begging. I'm going to write those, not flinch.

**The kids.** Maddie is nine and lying about something small all evening (she broke something, she has a crush, she snuck a video — I'll decide in scene). Eli is six and obsessed with a plastic triceratops named Gary. He talks about Gary a lot. Gary is going to end the story, not a scarf.

**The crew.** Four men, but I'm breaking the checklist. The "brute" is quiet and kind of sad. The "jumpy one" turns out to be the most dangerous. The leader isn't the scariest. One of them is going to survive. That's the problem she carries out.

**Plot shape.** Same bones as before — single night, single house, past catching up — but I'm disrupting the tidy one-kill-per-chapter rhythm. One kill will be ugly and go wrong in a non-cool way (she kills a neighbor who came to check on the noise; this happens and isn't undone). One antagonist walks out alive. The backstory stays partial — we get enough to understand, not enough to close.

**Voice & style.** Close third, past tense, rude when it needs to be. Short sentences, but I'll let a paragraph sprawl if the texture wants it. Some deliberately flat reportorial prose as contrast. Dialogue that's sometimes dumb, sometimes off-rhythm, not always a line. I'll open at least one chapter mid-action without orientation. I will not write "the night pressed in" sentences. I will not end on a poetic image that gestures at theme.

**What I'm cutting from the previous plan.** The knitting needles as kill weapon (too cute). The memorized phone number and cleanup crew (too *John Wick*). The three rules as a symmetrical payoff structure. The scarf-on-the-bus ending. Holloway's villain monologue about having made her. The tattoo reveal.

**What I'm keeping.** Suburban house, one night, crew of four, past-coming-for-her premise, the cookies, Maddie's perceptiveness, the morning after.

**What I'm aiming for.** A protagonist who is compelling because she's a little wrong. Violence that costs. An ending that doesn't absolve. The prompt's swagger delivered, but with residue.

# Chapter Planning

**Chapter 1 — The Mercers (~1000 words)**
Wren arrives at the Mercers' at seven. Establish house, kids, parents, the evening. Mrs. Mercer is a little drunk already and over-explains the microwave. Mr. Mercer is on his phone. Eli immediately introduces Gary the triceratops. Maddie is on a tablet and barely looks up; Wren can tell she's hiding something on the screen. Wren takes the cash advance, notes the alarm code, notes the back door doesn't latch right. After the parents leave she does what she always does — walks the house slow, opens a few drawers, reads the labels in the medicine cabinet, takes one Ativan and pockets it for later. Not tonight. She's working. Makes cookie dough with Eli, who narrates Gary's opinions on chocolate chips. Maddie stays on her tablet. A car passes twice on the street. Wren clocks it but doesn't react yet. End: she puts the kids to bed, sits on the couch, and sees the car again, parked now, lights off, three houses down.

**Chapter 2 — Dogs (~1000 words)**
She watches for a long time before moving. Four men get out. She recognizes the walk of one of them before she can see his face, and something in her stomach goes cold and familiar. She goes upstairs. Wakes Maddie first. Tells her: take your brother up to the attic and stay there, don't come down, don't make noise, I'll come get you. Maddie asks why. Wren says, "Because there are bad men." Maddie doesn't cry. She asks if she can bring the tablet. Wren says yes. Eli wakes asking for Gary; they find Gary; they go up. Wren doesn't call 911. She could. She doesn't, and she registers that about herself. She goes to the kitchen and takes the good knife out of the block, and a smaller paring knife, and slides the paring knife into her back waistband. The doorbell rings. Then again. Then the sound of someone walking around the side of the house. End: glass breaking at the back.

**Chapter 3 — Denny (~1000 words)**
The jumpy young one, Denny, comes through first — she expects the brute and is surprised; the surprise almost gets her killed. They struggle in the mudroom and he's fast, faster than she is, and stronger than he looks, and for thirty seconds it's a real question. She wins it ugly — slips on a boot, goes down, comes up under his jaw with the knife. He bleeds out on the tile making a sound she doesn't want to remember. Her hand is shaking. She makes herself stop it. The others heard — they had to have — and she waits for them to come and they don't. Silence. Then the leader's voice from somewhere in the house: *"Wren. Sweetheart. We just want to talk."* She doesn't know the voice. She knows the word sweetheart. End: she hears someone upstairs.

**Chapter 4 — Neighbor (~1000 words)**
Someone is moving on the second floor. She goes up in the dark, paring knife out, and at the top of the stairs she sees a figure in the hallway and she moves on it fast and quiet and puts the knife into its neck before she understands what she's looking at. It's Mr. Halvorsen from next door. Bathrobe. Flashlight. He must have heard the glass. He makes a sound and goes down. She catches him so he doesn't thump. She kneels there with him for a second that lasts longer than it should. She does not throw up. She wants to. She drags him into the linen closet and closes the door and her hands are wet and she wipes them on a towel that was folded nicely. When she comes out she is different. The prose should register this without saying it. From downstairs: *"Wren? You okay up there?"* The leader is fucking with her. She goes down.

**Chapter 5 — Ray (~1000 words)**
The middle-aged one — Ray — is in the kitchen, sitting at the island with his hands flat on the marble like someone waiting for a meal. He's unarmed, or pretending to be. He says he's out. He says he knew Denny was going to get himself killed. He says the leader — he calls him Cope, short for something — isn't right, hasn't been right for a long time, and he, Ray, has a daughter, and he's just driving tonight, he was just driving. Wren stands in the doorway with the knife and listens. She believes him about the daughter. She doesn't believe him about being out. She tells him to leave out the front door and not come back. He goes. She lets him. She doesn't know why and she tells herself it's because he didn't do anything yet and she knows that's a lie. Through the window she watches him walk to the SUV and get in and drive away. That's the man who lives. End: footsteps in the basement. And another set — the brute, Marco — somewhere on the main floor.

**Chapter 6 — Marco (~1000 words)**
She finds Marco in the laundry room. He is huge and he is crying, quietly, while he looks for her. He's been crying for a while. She doesn't understand it and doesn't want to. He sees her and says, "I'm sorry," and comes at her anyway. It is the worst fight of the night. He gets her against the dryer and she thinks *this is it* with a clarity that surprises her, and then her hand finds the iron on the shelf and she hits him with it until he stops. She keeps hitting after he stops, once, twice. That's the ugly beat I'm not flinching from. She sits on the floor next to him afterward for maybe a minute. Her forearm is opened up; she binds it with a dishtowel. Upstairs Eli is crying — she can hear it faintly through the vents. End: she goes to the basement door. Opens it. Goes down.

**Chapter 7 — Cope (~1000 words)**
Cope is waiting for her in the finished basement, sitting in the Mercers' recliner like he lives there. He is not what she expected. Older. Unimpressive. He says her name — not Wren, the other one, the one from before, and I'll leave that name unspoken on the page or mostly so. He doesn't monologue. He asks her how she's been. He asks about her mother. He tells her two or three specific things that place him in her life — small, domestic, wrong things, the kind of detail that says *I was there once and you didn't know me then.* She realizes he isn't the man she thinks should have come for her; he's someone lower down who volunteered. He wants the job because finishing her is a promotion. This is worse, somehow, than if it had been personal. He has a gun and he uses it and he misses once and hits her in the thigh the second time and she gets to him anyway because the basement is small and she is furious now in a way she hasn't let herself be all night. She kills him with her hands and the paring knife and it takes a while. She does not feel good afterward. She does not feel bad. She feels like she has finished a chore. End: she climbs the stairs.

**Chapter 8 — Gary (~1000 words)**
Dawn is coming but not here yet. She does not call a cleanup crew because she does not have a cleanup crew. She has a phone and 911 and a version of the story she starts assembling while she washes her hands: a home invasion, a neighbor who heroically came to help and was killed, a babysitter who fought back. It is not a perfect story. Some of it will hold. She will not be Wren anymore after tonight; she knows that. She goes upstairs and gets the kids down from the attic. Eli has Gary. Maddie looks at the blood on her and asks, flat, "Are they gone?" Wren says yes. Maddie nods like she's been told the weather. Wren puts them on the couch with a blanket and the TV on and goes to the kitchen and bakes the cookies they made last night, because she needs the house to smell like something else when the cops come, and because Eli will want one. When they come out of the oven Eli eats two and gives one to Gary. Maddie doesn't eat. She watches Wren. She says, "I won't tell." Wren doesn't ask what she means. She calls 911 at seven-fourteen. The parents come home to a police line. In the noise of it Wren slips away before they can find her to thank her — out the back, across the yard, through the gap in the hedge she noticed earlier. She walks. She doesn't take a bus. Her thigh is bleeding through the bandage. Somewhere a few blocks away she sits on a curb and realizes she's still holding Gary. Eli pressed him into her hand at some point and she didn't notice. End: she sits on the curb with a plastic dinosaur in her lap and tries to figure out what to do with him. That's the last image. Not resonant. Just true.
