# Wren

**Background.** Her real name isn't Wren. She was born into something — not a cartel, not a mafia, nothing with a name that would mean anything to a cop. A crew. Her stepfather ran it, and her mother kept the books and the quiet. Wren grew up in a house in the desert outside Yuma where men came and went and sometimes didn't come back, and by twelve she knew what the crawlspace under the kitchen was for. She started helping at fifteen, not by choice exactly — by gravity. She was good at it. She was good at it in a way that made her stepfather proud, which was the worst thing about it. At nineteen something happened that she doesn't narrate to herself anymore — she left in the middle of the night with a split lip and eleven hundred dollars from the safe, took a bus to Phoenix, then another to wherever, then another. She's been Wren for almost four years now. She babysits, does some cash under-the-table at a vet clinic cleaning kennels, rents a studio where the shower drains slow. She hasn't killed anyone in three years and eight months. She knows the exact number and doesn't like that she does.

**Personality.** Quiet in a way adults read as shy and kids read as listening. Dry. A little mean in her head and almost never out loud. She likes kids because kids don't perform and don't expect her to. She is lonely in a way she has decided not to address. She reads a lot — thrillers, mostly, which she finds funny. She cries at commercials sometimes and is embarrassed by it.

**Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Steals small things from the houses she sits in. Not valuables — a single Ativan from a bottle of thirty, a twenty off a dresser where there's a pile, a nice pen. She tells herself it's a tax on people who don't lock their cabinets. She knows this is bullshit. She reads the mail on the counter. She eats the parents' leftovers and doesn't hide it. She bites her thumbnail when she's thinking and the nail is always ragged. She flirts, sometimes, with dads, in microscopic ways she doesn't act on, and afterward dislikes herself about it for a day or two. She is not a good person who does one bad thing. She is a mostly okay person with a lot of small ugliness and one very large thing in her past.

**Physicality.** Five-six. Thin but not delicate — sinew, not grace. Dark hair she cuts herself in the bathroom and it shows. A face that ages depending on the light: seventeen in bad fluorescent, twenty-eight at 3 a.m. Jeans, a henley, beat-up Vans. She moves economically. She doesn't fidget. When she's scared her hands go very still and her jaw sets, which reads as calm to people who don't know better. She has a small scar under her chin from a kitchen knife when she was eleven and a long flat scar on her ribs she doesn't explain.

**Motives & allegiances.** Survive. Keep the kids alive. Get through the night without becoming the thing she was at nineteen, and failing that, get through the night.

**Voice.**
> *She'd read somewhere that you were supposed to narrate yourself through hard things. Pick up the knife. Walk to the door. Turn the knob. It was supposed to keep you present. She thought that was stupid. The trick was not being present.*

> "I'm not gonna hurt you, buddy. I just want you to go upstairs and stay with Gary, okay? Gary's scared. He needs you to be brave for him."

> *The Ativan was still in her pocket. She thought about it the way you think about a cigarette when you've quit.*

---

# Maddie Mercer

**Background.** Nine. Third-grader. Good at school, bad at friends. Only child until Eli came and then suddenly middle-management. Her parents love her and don't really see her; she has figured this out and is angry about it in a slow-growing way she doesn't have the vocabulary for yet. She spends a lot of time on her tablet and has recently, in the last two months, started watching things she isn't supposed to watch — a YouTube channel where a woman does true-crime recaps in a sweet voice. Maddie thinks about murder more than a nine-year-old probably should. Not doing it. Just — the fact of it. The way people do it and the way other people find out.

**Personality.** Watchful. Withholding. Funny when she wants to be. She tests people — small lies, small provocations, to see what they'll do. She likes Wren because Wren doesn't try. Most babysitters try.

**Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Lies about small things for practice. Tonight she has been hiding a broken figurine from her mother's shelf — she knocked it off Tuesday and glued it wrong and put it back hoping no one would notice. She's been thinking about it all week. She is a little cruel to Eli in ways he doesn't register yet. She bites the inside of her cheek. She is too old for her age in some ways and much younger in others.

**Physicality.** Tall for nine, coltish, brown hair in a messy ponytail she did herself. Glasses she pushes up with her knuckle. She holds the tablet like a shield. When she's scared she goes very quiet and very still, like her mother does when her father is mad, which is a thing she has learned without being taught.

**Motives & allegiances.** Herself. Eli, reluctantly. She will protect him tonight but she will also resent him for needing it.

**Voice.**
> "You said bad men. Are they here for us or for you?"

> *She knew she was supposed to be more scared. She was scared. But she was also — and she wouldn't have had the word for this — interested.*

> "I won't tell."

---

# Eli Mercer

**Background.** Six. Kindergarten. Loves dinosaurs with a focus that has worried his parents into a specialist appointment they haven't made yet. His whole inner life runs on Gary, a plastic triceratops his grandfather gave him, and Gary's complicated opinions about everything.

**Personality.** Sweet, chatty, absent from the main conversation and deep inside his own. Will ask you a question and then answer it himself before you can. Hugs hard.

**Idiosyncrasies.** Gary has a voice — higher than Eli's, a little raspy. Gary is grumpy and hates peas. Eli will not go to sleep without Gary on the pillow beside him. Eli knows the names of twelve dinosaurs and will recite them if given any excuse.

**Physicality.** Small, soft, pajamas with planets on them. Scab on one knee. Hair that sticks up in the back no matter what.

**Motives & allegiances.** Gary. His sister. His mom. Wren, now, a little.

**Voice.**
> "Gary says the cookies need more chips. Gary says that's the rule."

> "Is the lady a nice lady? Gary thinks she's a nice lady but Gary thinks everyone is a nice lady."

---

# Cope

**Background.** Fifty-one. Middle-rung for twenty-five years in an organization that has no name but has a shape. Never quite made the jump to the inner thing. Watched younger men get brought up while he stayed where he was. Volunteered for the Wren job because he's been told, not in so many words, that if he brings her in he's got a seat at a different table. He is aware this might not be true. He came anyway. He has been looking for her for ten months.

**Personality.** Patient. Methodical. Not cruel for sport but willing. Reads westerns. Has a wife in Henderson who thinks he's in freight.

**Idiosyncrasies.** Chews sunflower seeds constantly and keeps the shells in a folded paper towel in his pocket. Always. Even tonight. He knew Wren's mother a little, years ago — talked to her twice at a cookout. He remembers her being kind about his tie.

**Physicality.** Soft-bodied, unimpressive, the kind of man you don't look at twice at a gas station. Grey at the temples. Wears a Members Only jacket unironically. Small wet eyes.

**Motives.** The promotion. Finishing the job. Proving to someone, maybe himself, that he should have been brought up years ago.

**Voice.**
> "Your mother had a nice laugh. I only heard it the once. Somebody's birthday, I think."

> "I'm not gonna talk to you about your feelings, sweetheart. I don't have the time and neither do you."

---

# Denny

**Background.** Twenty-four. Fast, mean, a natural at it. The one in the crew who scares the others a little. No real backstory needed; he'd resist one if you tried. Dead by the end of Ch 3.

**Personality.** A grin that doesn't mean anything. Talks too much when he's nervous, which he always is, which is part of why he's dangerous — the nerves move faster than thought.

**Physicality.** Wiry, tattooed knuckles, cheap cologne. Moves like something that's been kicked a lot and learned from it.

**Voice.**
> "Aw, she's cute. Hey. Hey. Don't. Hey—"

---

# Marco

**Background.** Thirty-eight. Bouncer, briefly a fighter, a man who has hurt many people for money and has started, in the last year, not to sleep well. His mother died in April. He has not told anyone in the crew. He took this job because it was offered and he needed the money because the funeral cost more than he had.

**Personality.** Quiet. Slow. Not stupid; just deliberate. Polite to waitresses. Reads the Bible in a confused, occasional way.

**Physicality.** Six-four, thick, a body that has started to ache in the mornings. A soft face on a hard neck. Hands he keeps closed when he isn't using them, because open they look too gentle.

**Idiosyncrasy.** Crying tonight, quietly, while he looks for her. He doesn't know exactly why. He thinks it might be about his mother. He thinks it might be about what he knows they're here to do. He is going to do it anyway, which is the part that breaks him.

**Voice.**
> "I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry."

---

# Ray

**Background.** Forty-six. Driver, fixer, low-level. Has done enough bad things to lose track but none of them with his own hands if he can help it. Has a daughter, twelve, who lives with his ex-wife in Reno and thinks he sells industrial parts. He is not lying about her.

**Personality.** Tired. Funny in a dry way he doesn't use with these men. Knows he is the smartest one in the car and knows this is not a thing to advertise.

**Physicality.** Average everything. A face that forgets itself. Windbreaker. Keys on a carabiner.

**Motives.** Get through the night. Get home. He will walk out when Wren lets him and he will not look back and he will not tell anyone and he will also, eventually, do another job like this one, because that's what he does. She knows this when she lets him go. That's the weight of it.

**Voice.**
> "I'm gonna put my hands on the counter, okay? I'm gonna keep 'em there. You and me are gonna have a conversation like adults."

> "I got a kid. I know everybody says that. I really got one."

---

# Mr. Halvorsen

**Background.** Seventy-two. Retired high school shop teacher. Widower two years. Has been lonely in a way he is too proud to name. Hears glass break next door at eleven-forty on a Friday and puts on his robe and gets his big Maglite because someone has to check, and because in a small way he wants to be useful to somebody again.

**Physicality.** Thin, stooped, slippers. White hair still thick. Smells faintly of Old Spice and basement.

**His role in the story.** He is killed by Wren in the upstairs hallway in the dark before either of them understands what's happening. He gets a paragraph of life before he dies and that is the whole point — that he was a person, not a beat. His death is the worst thing she does tonight and she knows it and the story will not redeem it.

# Chapter 1 — The Mercers

The Mercers lived in one of those houses that looked bigger from the street than it was inside. Pale brick, two stories, a lawn kept by someone else. Wren parked her Civic at the curb because the driveway was full and walked up with her bag on her shoulder, bag strap across her chest the way she always wore it, hand on the strap. She rang the bell at six fifty-eight. She liked to be two minutes early. Any earlier and people felt surveilled; any later and they started the evening tense.

Mrs. Mercer opened the door already holding a glass of white. She was a pretty woman gone slightly loose at the edges, a caterer's wife with a caterer's husband. "Wren, hi, hi, come in, we're running so late, Greg — Greg, Wren's here — Wren, you look nice, did you do something to your hair?"

"No," Wren said.

"It looks nice."

The house smelled like the candle she knew from the Target by the freeway. Eli came around the corner at a full run in pajamas with planets on them, stopped two feet from her knees, and held up a plastic triceratops.

"This is Gary," he said.

"Hi, Gary."

"Gary says hi back but he's shy."

"That's okay."

"Gary doesn't like it when people look at him too long."

"I'll try not to."

Maddie was on the couch with a tablet angled away from the room. She looked up without moving her head, registered Wren, went back to the screen. Wren saw in the second before the glance broke that she had her thumb over whatever was in the corner of the screen, hiding it. Not porn. A kid that age hiding porn wouldn't be that practiced. Something else.

"Kitchen," Mrs. Mercer said. "Come. Let me show you the — I know I showed you last time, but Greg redid the — "

"Microwave," Wren said.

"Microwave, right, right, you have to press clear first or it won't — "

"I remember."

Mr. Mercer came down the stairs tying a tie and saying something into his phone. He smiled at Wren without looking at her. He was handsome in a way that had begun, very recently, to stop being handsome. He put his hand over the phone and said, "Cash on the counter. Ninety for tonight, we'll be back by midnight-thirty, one at the latest, it's the thing at the Drury."

"Great," Wren said.

"Kids have eaten. Maddie's not allowed on the tablet after nine."

"Okay."

"She'll say she is. She's not."

"Okay."

He went back to his phone. Mrs. Mercer hugged her children like she wouldn't see them for a week, kissed the tops of their heads, left lipstick on Eli. Then they were gone in a wash of perfume and keys and the door shut too hard and the house adjusted around the absence.

Wren stood in the front hall and listened.

Refrigerator. The tablet. Eli narrating something to Gary in a whisper. A car on the cross street. Nothing else.

"Okay," she said, mostly to herself.

She did her walk. She did it in every house. She told herself it was so she'd know the layout if something happened, and that was true and also not the whole truth. She went room to room slow, opening the doors she was allowed to open and one or two she wasn't. Master bedroom: unmade on his side, made on hers. A pile of bills by the window. A twenty on the dresser with a receipt under it; she left the twenty. The medicine cabinet in the master bath had the usual — floss, a prescription for something heart-related in his name, Zoloft in hers, a bottle of Ativan with her name on it and thirty in the count. Wren took one. She palmed it and dropped it in the watch pocket of her jeans. Not for tonight. She didn't take things the night she took them.

Back of the house: sliding door onto a little deck, then grass, then a line of trees. She checked the lock. The latch rode a quarter inch short of the strike. She lifted the handle and pressed and heard the bolt go. Fine if you knew. Most people didn't know.

Front door: deadbolt worked. Alarm panel by the coat closet. The code was on a Post-it inside the cabinet above the microwave, which was its own problem, but not hers tonight.

She came back to the kitchen. Eli was on the stool with his elbows on the island and Gary lying on his side next to a bag of chocolate chips.

"We're making cookies," Eli said.

"Are we."

"Gary says we have to."

"Well."

"Gary says you have to use more than the recipe says. He says recipes are the minimum."

"Gary's a strong personality."

"Yeah."

She got the bowl down and the butter from the counter where Mrs. Mercer had left it softening, and they made dough. Eli measured the sugar with both hands on the cup like it was heavy. He told her Gary's opinions on each ingredient. She let him crack the egg and she picked the shell out of the bowl without him seeing because he would've been upset. Maddie stayed on the couch. At one point Wren looked over and Maddie was looking at her, not at the tablet, with a small flat expression Wren couldn't read, and then the tablet again.

They put the dough in the fridge to bake later. Teeth, pajamas, a book. Eli wanted the one about the moon; she read it. Maddie took herself to bed without being asked and closed her door firmly.

Wren sat on the couch in the living room with the television low and her bag at her feet. At nine-forty a car came slowly down the street with its headlights on and kept going. At ten-fifteen the same car came back the other way and kept going.

At ten-fifty-two it came back and stopped.

She watched the headlights go out.

# Chapter 2 — Dogs

She watched for a long time before she moved.

This was something her stepfather had taught her, although he hadn't put it in words. You watched. You let the other person commit to being there before you committed to seeing them. Amateurs looked and then acted. Professionals looked and kept looking and then, when they had enough, acted once.

The SUV was a dark Tahoe, older, three houses down on the opposite side. The driver killed the lights but not the engine, not for a full minute. The engine cut. Nobody got out for another minute after that. Then the driver's door, then the passenger, then the back two almost together. Four men. They stood on the sidewalk for a second arranging themselves the way a crew does — checking who was carrying what, who was going where — and that was what told her, more than anything else, what they were. Civilians didn't stand like that on a sidewalk.

The tallest one rolled his neck and it popped loud enough that she could almost hear it through the glass.

She knew the walk of the one on the left. Not the face — too far, too dark — but the walk, the way he led with his right shoulder like he was about to turn into a door that wasn't there. She had watched a man walk that way across a kitchen in Yuma for half her childhood. Not him; he was dead. Someone who had learned from the same person, or from him.

Something in her stomach went cold and familiar, the way a room you haven't been in for years is still the shape of itself in the dark.

She stood up. She did not hurry. Hurry was how you forgot things.

Upstairs first. Maddie's door. She went in without knocking and sat on the edge of the bed and put her hand on Maddie's shoulder and Maddie came awake all at once, eyes open, not startled, like she had been waiting to be woken.

"Hey," Wren said, quiet. "I need you to listen to me and not ask questions until I'm done."

Maddie nodded.

"There are bad men about to come in the house. I need you to take your brother up to the attic, the crawlspace off the landing, and close the hatch. You know the one."

"Yeah."

"You stay up there no matter what you hear. You don't come down. You don't peek. If you hear me and it doesn't sound right, you stay up there anyway. You understand me?"

"Yeah."

"If I don't come for you — if nobody you know comes — you wait until it's light and then you go out the front and across to the Halvorsens'. Only the Halvorsens'. Not the house with the dogs."

"Okay."

"Repeat it."

"Attic. Stay. Don't come down. Halvorsens' in the morning."

"Good."

Maddie sat up. She reached for her glasses and got them on. Then she said, "Can I bring my tablet?"

Wren almost laughed. "Yes. Bring the tablet. Keep it on silent. Do not turn the flashlight on."

"Okay."

"Get your brother. Be quiet with him."

Eli was harder. He was a deep sleeper and he was six, and he came up fuzzy and whiny, and when Maddie said *come on Eli we're doing a game* he said he didn't want to and Wren crouched by the bed and said, "Buddy. Where's Gary?"

"Under the pillow."

"Get Gary. Gary has to come."

"Why?"

"Gary's scared. He wants to go with you."

That worked. He clutched Gary to his chest and let his sister take his hand and Wren walked them to the landing and pulled the cord on the attic hatch and the little folding stairs came down and she lifted Eli up first because his legs wouldn't do the climb on their own. Then Maddie. Maddie paused on the third step and looked down at Wren and said, with the same flat voice as before, "Are they here for us or for you?"

"Go," Wren said.

Maddie went.

Wren folded the stairs back up and pushed the hatch closed and wiped a smudge of dust off the ceiling with her sleeve.

Then she stood on the landing and did not move for maybe five seconds and thought about the phone in her pocket.

She could call 911. The cops in this town were four minutes away. Four minutes was a long time and also not that long. She could call and stand in the hallway with a knife and wait. She could tell them the truth — four men are coming in my employer's house — and they would come, and the men outside would see the cars and leave, and she would be on a report, and her name and the photo from her driver's license would be on a report, and somewhere an office would flag it, and the rest of her life would be a different length than it had been ten minutes ago.

She did not call.

She registered, distantly, that she hadn't called. She registered that she had known, coming up the stairs, that she was not going to call. She filed this away to think about later, if there was a later.

She went down to the kitchen.

She pulled the good eight-inch from the block and tested the edge against her thumbnail. It shaved. Mr. Mercer kept his knives sharp; one of the things she liked about him. She took the paring knife too, four-inch, and slid it handle-down into the back waistband of her jeans where the henley would cover it.

She killed the kitchen light. She killed the living-room lamp. She left the television on, low, because a dark house without sound would tell them something the television wouldn't.

The doorbell rang.

She stood very still in the dark hallway and watched the frosted glass beside the door. A shape on the porch. Then the bell again, polite, like a neighbor. Then the sound of a man walking slowly around the side of the house, footsteps in the mulch, casual, in no hurry at all.

From the back of the house, glass broke.

# Chapter 3 — Denny

The glass went in two pieces — the first a short hard snap, the second a longer slumping fall as whoever it was reached through and swept the shards out of the frame so they wouldn't catch on his sleeve. Somebody who had done it before. Somebody who hadn't, in her experience, done it very many times.

She was already in the mudroom.

The mudroom was a narrow run between the kitchen and the back door, hooks on one wall, a bench with cubbies on the other, a washer-dryer stack at the far end, the back door itself centered. There was a window in the back door and that was the window that had gone. She had tucked herself in against the washer with the eight-inch held low along her thigh and her breath pushed down into her stomach where it wouldn't show.

She had been expecting the big one. The tall one who rolled his neck. That was how she had placed him in her head — first through the door, because the big ones always were, because the crew sent the body in first and the brain in second. She had placed him in her head and she had placed the knife accordingly, up high under the jaw, because going for the body on someone that size was wasted work.

It wasn't him.

It was a skinny kid with tattooed knuckles, a cheap-cologne smell that reached her before he did, a black hoodie, a grin already on his face for no reason she could see. He came through the doorframe sideways because he was narrow enough to and because he was quick. He was quick. That was the first thing she understood, and the second thing she understood was that she had miscalibrated, and the third thing she understood was that her body had already committed to the jaw-strike geometry of a different, larger man and was wrong about everything.

He saw her and said, "Aw, she's cute."

She went for him anyway.

The knife went where she had sent it and met nothing — he was not where a bigger man would have been, he was lower, faster, under the swing, and her wrist passed over his shoulder and she was fouled against her own momentum. He came up into her with his forearm under her chin and drove her back into the washer hard enough that the whole stack rocked and a detergent bottle on top fell and bounced.

The knife was still in her hand. She felt that. She told herself to remember that.

He got a fistful of her hair and yanked and her feet came off the ground for a second and she thought, clearly, *he's going to kill me by accident.* Not by plan. He was going to get too excited and break something he wasn't supposed to break.

She kicked the side of his knee.

She got it clean. He buckled and she came down with him and they went to the floor together in the narrow space between the bench and the washer and he was still grinning — actually grinning — and saying, "Hey. Hey. Hey, don't — *hey* — " in a voice that was almost laughing.

He got a hand on the wrist of her knife hand.

This was the part she didn't like. He was stronger than her. Not by a lot. By enough. She felt him start to peel her wrist open and she felt her fingers start to go and she let her arm go slack for half a second, a half second she counted, and he overcommitted — pulled where he didn't need to pull — and she brought her knee up between them and rolled her hip and came out the other side of him, ugly, scraping an elbow on the bench, and now he was the one half-under the washer and she was the one with leverage.

She couldn't get the eight-inch around. The angle was wrong.

She reached behind her, left-handed, and got the paring knife.

He saw it. He had a half-second to see it. In that half-second his face did something that wasn't quite fear — it was closer to surprise, like a kid who has been told a rule he didn't know existed. His grin stayed on his mouth but his eyes left it.

She put the paring knife into the side of his neck under the jaw.

It went in easier than she remembered. She had forgotten how little resistance there was when you hit the soft part between the muscle and the bone. She had forgotten and she was grateful, for one second, that she had forgotten, and then she was ashamed of being grateful.

He made a sound.

It wasn't a scream. It was a noise she didn't have a word for — wet, surprised, almost polite, like someone clearing his throat at a funeral. He kicked one leg out and his heel hit the washer twice, *bam bam*, before she got her forearm across his mouth and held it there. His eyes found hers and held on and then stopped holding on and then were just eyes.

It took longer than it should have. It always did.

When he was finished she pulled the paring knife out and wiped it on his hoodie and sat back on her heels and looked at her hand. Her hand was shaking. It was shaking enough that she watched it for a full breath, the way you watch something that is not yours, and then she set the knife on the floor and put her hand flat on the tile and pressed down until the shaking went into the tile and stopped.

She stood up.

There was blood on her henley from collarbone to hem on the left side. There was blood on the washer. There was blood on the detergent bottle, which was still bouncing in a slow diminishing arc at the edge of the bench.

The house was quiet.

The others had heard. They had to have heard the washer, at least. She listened for movement and got none, and that was worse than movement, because it meant they were standing still and listening for her the same way.

Then a voice came from somewhere in the front of the house — not loud, conversational, a man in a living room calling to a woman in the kitchen.

"Wren. Sweetheart. We just want to talk."

She didn't know the voice.

She knew the word *sweetheart.*

# Chapter 4 — Neighbor

She did not answer.

The voice had come from the front of the house and she stood in the mudroom in the dark and let it sit on the air until it was gone. Answering was what he wanted. He was putting a line out to see where she pulled from. She did not pull.

She stepped over Denny without looking at him and went into the kitchen low. The television in the living room was still on, muted blue light pulsing into the hall. She kept the island between her and the front of the house and went to the breaker panel in the pantry and opened it one-handed and put her fingers on the main and stopped.

No. The TV was cover. Without the TV the house became a listening chamber and he would hear her moving. Leave the power.

She closed the panel.

She went back through the kitchen and up the back stairs.

The back stairs were narrow and carpeted and came up behind the laundry closet on the second floor, between Eli's room and the bathroom. She went up on the outside edges of the treads where they were tight against the stringer and wouldn't creak. Her mother's trick. Her mother had known every quiet place in every floor of every house they'd lived in and she had shown Wren, not like a lesson, just walking through rooms saying *not here, not here, here's fine.*

At the top she crouched. She listened.

The front of the house was where the voice had been. The voice had come from near the foyer, she thought, maybe the bottom of the main stairs. That man had a gun or he didn't. She had to assume he did. Denny hadn't. Denny had come in with hands. That meant either Denny was the throwaway or the crew wasn't heavy on firearms or both. She filed it.

She moved down the upstairs hall toward the landing. The landing was where the main stairs came up and where the attic hatch was and where — she saw this before she understood she was seeing it — a figure stood with its back to her.

A figure with a flashlight.

The flashlight was pointed down at the carpet, not up, not swinging, and that was the thing that got her moving before her brain caught up. A man clearing a house swept a flashlight. This one was held down like somebody who didn't want to wake a kid.

She crossed the ten feet between them without sound.

She had the paring knife in her right hand because the paring knife was what was in her right hand. She put her left hand over his mouth from behind and she put the paring knife into the side of his neck in the same place she had put it into Denny's, because that was the place she knew now, and he made a small noise against her palm and his knees went.

He was light.

That was what she noticed first. He was light in a way Denny had not been light. Denny had been a hundred and sixty pounds of quick. This man was less than that and softer and his shoulders under her hand were thin and bony and the robe — the *robe* —

She knew before she turned him.

She held him against her chest and let him down slow because she had taught herself, a long time ago, not to let bodies fall. Bodies falling made noise. She went to her knees with him and laid him on his back on the carpet of the upstairs hall and the flashlight rolled out of his hand and the beam went across his face and she saw him.

Mr. Halvorsen from next door.

White hair. The robe she had seen him in once in August, watering his tomatoes at dusk. Slippers. One slipper had come off on the stairs, she saw now, looking back; it sat on the third step up from the landing like something a child had dropped.

His eyes were open and he was trying to say something and nothing was coming out except a soft wet sound and a lot of blood, a great deal of blood, more blood than she would have thought a man his age had in him. His hand came up and found her wrist and held on. Not hard. Just held.

She said, "I'm sorry."

She said it out loud. She heard herself say it.

His hand stayed on her wrist for maybe six seconds and then it didn't.

She sat back on her heels on the hallway carpet and looked at him. The flashlight beam was still pointed at the wainscoting and the wainscoting was lit up in a warm clean circle that had nothing to do with anything. She reached out and clicked the flashlight off. Then she took her hand off it because her hand had left a print on the metal in Denny's blood, and there was nothing to be done about that, and she registered it and filed it and moved on.

She did not throw up. She wanted to. She wanted to very badly. She swallowed twice and breathed through her nose and the wanting moved down into her stomach and stayed there like something she would carry for a long time.

She put her hands under his arms and dragged him across the hall to the linen closet. He was not heavy. His heels made two long smears on the carpet and she looked at the smears and thought, *that's fine, that's fine, that was always going to happen.* She opened the closet door and pulled him in and folded his legs in after him and closed the door.

The towels on the shelf were folded with the rounded edges out. Mrs. Mercer folded towels like that. Wren took one off the top of the stack and wiped her hands on it, both sides, and then put the towel in the closet with him and shut the door again.

She stood up.

From downstairs the voice came again, patient, pleasant, like a man calling for a cat.

"Wren? You okay up there?"

She stood in the hallway in the dark with her palms still tacky and the paring knife down at her side and she understood, with a clarity that had not been there before Mr. Halvorsen, that she was going to kill every one of them who did not run.

She went down the main stairs.

# Chapter 5 — Ray

The main stairs came down into the foyer and the foyer opened into the kitchen on the right and the living room on the left. She came down on the outside edges again and stopped three from the bottom and listened.

Living room: empty. The TV light alone.

Kitchen: a man at the island.

She could see him through the doorway at an angle, just his hands and the near edge of his shoulder. The hands were flat on the marble like someone waiting to be served. She watched them for a ten-count. They did not move. The fingers did not drum. He was not reaching under the counter. He was sitting still on purpose so she would see him sitting still.

She came down the last three steps and crossed the foyer and stood in the kitchen doorway with the paring knife at her hip.

He was in his forties. Plain face. Windbreaker zipped halfway. Keys on a carabiner clipped through his belt loop. He had turned on the light over the range, not the main lights — a dim warm bulb over the stove. He had done this, she understood, so she could see him without being inside the light herself. A small courtesy.

He saw her and did not move his hands.

"Hey," he said.

She didn't answer.

"I'm Ray. I'm gonna put my hands on the counter, okay? I'm gonna keep 'em there. You and me are gonna have a conversation like adults."

"Your hands are already on the counter."

"Yeah. They're gonna stay there."

"Where's the other one?"

"Basement, last I knew. Cope's in the basement. Marco was coming up the main. I don't know where Marco is right now. I'm not lying to you about that."

"Denny's in the mudroom."

Ray exhaled through his nose. "Figured."

"You knew it was gonna be him."

"I knew he was gonna go first through the door because that's what he does. Did. Yeah."

She took a step into the kitchen. He watched her feet, not her face. That was smart. Faces lied; feet told you what someone was about to do.

"Talk," she said.

"I'm out."

"Sure."

"I mean it. I'm driving tonight. That's the deal. I drove them here and I'm supposed to drive them back, that's the whole — that's what I'm here for. I didn't come in with hands. Check me if you want, I got a folding knife in my pocket and nothing else, you can have the knife."

"I don't want your knife."

"Okay."

She came another step in. She could see the whole kitchen now. Nobody under the island. The pantry door was open the way she had left it. No boots showing under the pantry.

"Why'd you sit down," she said.

"Because I was gonna get killed if I didn't."

"Correct."

"Yeah."

"Keep talking."

"Cope's not right. I'm telling you this because it's true and also because it's the only thing I got that's worth something to you. He's been wrong for a year. He volunteered for this because somebody told him if he brought you in he'd get moved up, and he believed it, and I don't think the person who told him meant it. I think they sent him because he'd go."

"How many of you know my name."

Ray's hands were still flat. "He does. Marco doesn't. Denny didn't. I — I know the one he calls you."

"Which one."

He said a name. Not loud. It landed in the room like a dropped cup.

She did not react. She had taught herself this a long time ago and she was grateful, now, that she had. Her face stayed where it was. Her hand on the knife stayed where it was. Inside her chest something cold moved a quarter inch and stopped.

"Nobody's called me that in four years," she said.

"I know."

"Who told him."

"I don't know. I don't. I'd tell you if I did. I'm telling you everything I got."

"You have a daughter."

"Yeah."

"How old."

"Twelve."

"Name."

"Kaylee."

"You're lying about the name."

"I'm not. I'm not lying about the kid and I'm not lying about the name. Everybody says they got a kid and I really got one. She lives with her mom in Reno. She thinks I sell industrial parts."

"What do you sell."

"Whatever somebody needs moved."

"Have you ever hurt a kid."

"No."

"Think about it before you answer."

"I already thought about it. No."

She looked at him for a long moment. He looked back only as much as he had to. His eyes kept finding the range hood above his head and coming back to her and finding the range hood again. She recognized the behavior. It was what people did when they were telling the truth and hated how it sounded.

"Walk out the front," she said.

He didn't move.

"Go," she said.

"You're not gonna — "

"If you turn around I will. If you come back I will. If I ever see you again, Ray, anywhere, a gas station in another state, I will. You go home to Reno and you tell your daughter you sell industrial parts and you keep selling them, whatever that means, and you stay out of my weather."

"Yeah."

"Get up slow."

He got up slow. He kept his hands visible the whole way. He walked past her with a yard of space and did not turn his back until he had to, at the front door, and then he turned it and opened the door and stepped out onto the porch and pulled the door shut behind him with a quietness that was its own apology.

She went to the window beside the door and watched him walk to the Tahoe. He walked like a man who was trying not to hurry and failing a little. He got in. He started it. He pulled away from the curb without the headlights on and turned them on at the end of the block.

She stood at the window and watched until the taillights were gone.

She knew, watching them go, that she had just let a man who did this for a living walk back out into the world to do it for a living. She knew what that meant. She filed it with Mr. Halvorsen and the towel and the smears on the carpet, on the shelf inside her where these things went.

From the laundry room, at the back of the house, she heard a man crying.

# Chapter 6 — Marco

The crying was quiet. That was the thing about it. It wasn't loud enough to be a trick and it wasn't soft enough to be private. It was a man trying not to cry and failing at a low volume, the way a man cries when he has been crying for a while and has given up expecting it to stop.

She moved along the back hall toward the laundry room with the eight-inch in her right hand and the paring knife in the back of her waistband again. She had rinsed the paring knife in the kitchen sink while she watched Ray's taillights. She had done it without thinking about it and only afterward registered that she had done it, and the registering had made her feel something she set aside to feel later, if later came.

The laundry room was at the end of the back hall, past the mudroom where Denny was. The door was open. The light inside was on — the overhead fluorescent, the cheap one that buzzed. She could see his shadow moving across the light under the door crack before she got close enough to see him. A big shadow. Slow.

She stopped three feet from the doorway.

She listened.

The crying. His breath. A small sound that she took a second to place and then placed: he was sniffing, trying to clear his nose, quietly, again and again. Like a man on a pew.

She stepped into the doorway.

He was standing in the middle of the little room with his back to her and his head down and he was not looking for her at all. He was just standing there. His shoulders were as wide as the space between the washer and the folding counter. He had a tire iron in his right hand, down at his thigh, and his left hand was up at his face, under his nose, and he was wiping his nose with the back of his wrist in a slow methodical way.

She said, "Turn around."

He turned around.

His face was red and wet and his eyes were very small in it. He was older than she had expected. Not by a lot. By five or six years. The kind of five or six years that showed in the way a body held itself more than in the face. His mouth had a shape to it that wasn't a sneer and wasn't a grimace. It was the mouth of a man who had known, walking into a room, that he was not going to walk out of it the same, and who had walked in anyway.

He said, "I'm sorry."

"Put it down."

"I can't."

"Put it down, Marco."

"I can't. I'm sorry. I can't."

He came at her.

He came at her slow for the first step and fast for the second, and she was already moving back out of the doorway because she had known he would, because the *I'm sorry* had been a man telling her what he was about to do and asking forgiveness for it in advance. She backed into the hall and he came through the doorway sideways because he had to and swung the tire iron low, at her knee, and she got the leg back and the iron passed and hit the doorframe and took a chunk of molding off the jamb.

He was strong. That part she had been right about. The way he moved after a swing was not the way a big slow man moved; it was the way a fighter moved, a man who had once made his living with his hands and had not forgotten the geometry. He recovered the iron and stepped into her and she had to give ground, and giving ground took her back down the hall into the kitchen and the kitchen was where it went wrong.

She tried to put the island between them.

He was faster around the island than she had counted on. He cut the corner. He got a hand on the collar of her henley and she felt the seam give at the shoulder and then his other hand, the one with the iron, came around and she got her forearm up and the iron hit her forearm instead of her temple and the forearm opened along the bone from elbow to wrist in a long bright line that did not hurt yet and would hurt in about four seconds.

He drove her back.

She hit the range with her hip and her hand went out for balance and found the handle of a skillet on the back burner and closed on it without her deciding, and she swung the skillet up into the side of his head with everything she had in her shoulder.

It was a cast-iron skillet. Mrs. Mercer seasoned it on Sundays.

It connected with his temple and the sound it made was not a sound she wanted. He went sideways into the refrigerator and the refrigerator rocked and a magnet fell and a child's drawing came with it. He stayed on his feet. He stayed on his feet and turned back toward her with his eyes not quite finding her and the tire iron still in his hand and she understood that the skillet had been the best hit she had in her and it had not been enough.

She hit him again.

She hit him in the same place and this time his legs went and he came down against the cabinets and slid. The tire iron left his hand and hit the floor and rolled under the oven.

He was breathing. He was looking up at her. His mouth was working around words that weren't coming.

She hit him again. With the skillet. In the head.

He stopped looking up at her.

She hit him once more after that. She did not need to. She registered, as the skillet came down, that she did not need to, and she brought it down anyway, and she felt, in the second her arm was at the top of the swing, something that was not satisfaction and was not anger and was not relief. It was close to all three and was none of them. It was the thing she had carried out of Yuma and pretended she had left behind.

She set the skillet on the stove.

She sat down on the kitchen floor next to Marco with her back against the cabinet and she looked at her forearm. It was open from the elbow to the wrist and the blood was coming in a steady unhurried pulse that told her she had missed the artery by a finger's width. She pulled the dishtowel off the oven handle and put it against her arm and held it there with her other hand and her teeth.

From the vent above the stove, faint, carried down through the ductwork from the attic two floors up, she heard Eli crying.

She sat there another five seconds and then she got up and went to the basement door.

# Chapter 7 — Cope

The basement door was in the back hall between the laundry room and the powder room. It was already open an inch. He had done that. She stood in front of it with the dishtowel tied around her forearm by its corners, pulled tight with her teeth and her good hand, and she put the eight-inch on the hallway sideboard because the eight-inch was too long for a staircase. She kept the paring knife.

She went down.

The stairs were carpeted and turned once at a landing. She took them slow. Light from below, not overhead — a lamp. He had turned on a lamp. She could smell him before she saw him. Sunflower shells and Old Spice aftershave and something sourer underneath, maybe sweat, maybe just old man.

She came off the last stair into the finished half of the basement.

He was sitting in the Mercers' recliner.

The recliner was angled at the foot of the stairs so that whoever came down came down into his line of sight. He was sitting in it with his legs crossed at the knee and a paper towel folded on his thigh and a pistol resting on the paper towel, not pointed at her, not in his hand, just sitting there where she could see it. His other hand had sunflower seeds in it. He was working them. One at a time. The shells went into a second folded paper towel on the armrest.

He was smaller than she had expected. Softer. Fifty-some, grey at the temples, a Members Only jacket zipped to the sternum. A face you'd forget at a gas station.

He said, "There you are."

She didn't answer.

"Sit down. There's the ottoman."

"No."

"Suit yourself."

He cracked a seed. He spit the shell into the paper towel. He did not look at the pistol and did not look at her hand with the paring knife. He looked at her face, patient, the way a man at a bus stop looks at the bus he expects.

"I knew your mother a little," he said.

She stayed where she was.

"Not well. I want to be clear about that. I met her twice. Somebody's birthday. Ramirez's kid, I think. You would've been nine, ten. I talked to her about a tie. I had on a tie I didn't like and she said something nice about it and I remembered that because I was having a bad day and she didn't know it and she was kind about the tie anyway. That's all. I'm not claiming I knew her."

She said, "Is this where you tell me she talked about me."

"No. She didn't. I don't know what she talked about when she wasn't talking about a tie."

"Good."

He nodded like she had scored a point fairly. He cracked another seed.

"I'm not here to have a conversation with you about your feelings, sweetheart. I don't have the time and neither do you. I'm just telling you why I recognized the name. When it came up I recognized the name and I put my hand up for it."

"You volunteered."

"Yeah."

"For a promotion."

"That's right."

"You think they're gonna give it to you."

He considered that. He cracked a seed.

"I think there's a chance," he said. "I think the chance isn't as big as the man who told me implied. I think I came anyway because I'm fifty-one and the chance of anything is smaller every year and a small chance is still a chance. I think you already knew all of that before I said it."

"Yeah."

"So."

He uncrossed his legs and recrossed them the other way and picked up the pistol off the paper towel. He did it slow. He did not point it at her. He held it loose in his lap with the muzzle at the carpet.

He said her other name.

Not loud. He said it the way he'd said *tie.* A small domestic word he happened to know. He said it and watched her face to see what happened to it and nothing did, and he nodded, a little, like he had expected that and was confirming it.

"I don't need you to come quiet," he said. "I want to be clear. I'm not asking."

"Okay."

"I just wanted to say the name out loud once before we did this. I've had it in my head for a while."

"Okay."

"All right."

He raised the pistol.

She was already moving. The basement was small and the recliner was four steps from the foot of the stairs and four steps was nothing, four steps was a held breath, and she closed two of them before the first shot and the first shot went past her left ear and into the drywall behind her and the second shot came as she was inside his arm and it went through the meat of her thigh, the outside of it, and she felt it go in and out, a bright punched feeling, and her leg kept working because adrenaline is a liar that tells useful lies.

She got the paring knife into his hand that had the pistol. Through the back of it, into the meat between the knuckles, and he made a noise and the pistol went sideways and she got her other hand on his throat.

He was not a big man.

She had been a big man's daughter and she knew what a big man felt like under a hand and he did not feel like one. She put her weight down through her palm into the soft under his jaw and she leaned and she did not let up.

He hit her. He hit her in the ribs twice and in the side of the head once and the hits were the hits of a man whose hands had mostly held paperwork for ten years. She took them. She kept leaning.

He tried to say something.

She did not let him.

It took longer than Denny and longer than Mr. Halvorsen and longer than Marco. It took a long time. He looked at her the whole way through and his eyes did not go to fear, which surprised her, they went to something more like disappointment, like a man who had bet on a horse and watched it come in second, and at the end his hand came up one more time and touched her wrist, not hard, almost the way Mr. Halvorsen had, and then it stopped touching her wrist.

She stayed on top of him a long moment after he stopped.

Then she got off him.

She sat on the ottoman and looked at her leg. The jeans were black with it. She untied the dishtowel from her forearm and retied it around her thigh above the hole, high and tight, and used her teeth again. The forearm started bleeding again. She didn't have another towel.

The paper towel with the sunflower shells was still folded on the armrest.

She left it there.

She got up and went to the stairs.

# Chapter 8 — Gary

She went up the stairs one at a time with her good hand on the rail and the bad leg trailing. Halfway up she had to stop and breathe with her forehead against the wall. The wall was cool. She stayed there longer than she meant to.

She was not going to call a cleanup crew because she did not have a cleanup crew. She had never had one. The number she had carried in her head for four years was a number she had never dialed because dialing it meant being found, and she had chosen, every morning for four years, not to be found.

She was going to call 911.

She worked on the story while she climbed. Home invasion. Four men. The neighbor heard glass and came to help and was killed in the upstairs hall. The babysitter fought back with a kitchen knife and got lucky. The babysitter's name, on the report, would be Wren Adler because that was the name on her license and the license was real enough to pass the kind of look a small-town detective would give it. After tonight she would not be Wren Adler. She knew that. She was already, standing on the staircase, composing the face she would show a paramedic and deciding what would come off it, later, when she threw the face away.

She came up into the kitchen. Marco was where she had left him. She stepped around him. She did not look at him long.

In the upstairs hall she stood under the attic hatch and pulled the cord. The folding stairs came down and she called up, not loud, "It's me. It's over."

Nothing for a second.

Then Maddie's face at the edge of the hatch. Glasses on. Tablet under her arm. She looked down at Wren and saw the leg and the arm and the shirt and did not react to any of it. She climbed down the folding stairs on her own and turned at the bottom and reached up for Eli, who came down after her with Gary pressed against his cheek.

Eli saw Wren and said, "You're red."

"Yeah, buddy."

"A lot."

"I know."

Maddie said, "Are they gone."

"Yeah."

"All of them."

"Yeah."

She said it evenly because Maddie was asking a specific question and deserved a specific answer, and Maddie received the answer the way she had received everything tonight, with a small nod that cost her nothing visible.

Wren walked them down the main stairs, slow, her hand on Eli's shoulder for balance as much as for him. She took them past the foyer — there was nothing in the foyer — and into the living room and sat them on the couch and pulled the throw blanket off the back and put it over their laps. She turned the TV off the news channel it had drifted to and found cartoons. She did not remember turning the TV to the news channel. Somebody had, at some point. Maybe her. Maybe him.

"I need you to stay here," she said. "I need you to stay on this couch and watch this and not get up. Not for anything. Not to look, not for water, not for the bathroom. If you need the bathroom you tell me and I'll take you."

Maddie said, "Okay."

Eli said, "Can Gary watch too."

"Gary has to watch. Gary's in charge."

"Okay."

She went to the kitchen. She pulled the tray of cookie dough out of the fridge. She set the oven to three-fifty and waited for it to beep and in the waiting she stood at the sink and washed her hands and arms up to the elbow in water as hot as she could stand. The water went pink and then clear and then pink again from the forearm, which was still going. She retied the dishtowel. She washed her face. She did not look in the window above the sink at her reflection because she did not want to meet her own eyes yet.

She put the cookies in.

She called 911 at seven-fourteen.

She told the dispatcher there had been a home invasion and that men had broken in and that she thought they were all down but she wasn't sure and that there were two children in the living room and that the neighbor had come over to help and the neighbor was upstairs and she didn't think the neighbor had made it. She said this in a voice that shook in the right places. Some of the shake was acting and some of it wasn't and by the end she had lost track of which was which.

The dispatcher told her to stay on the line.

She stayed on the line.

The cookies came out at seven-twenty-two. She took them off the tray with a spatula and put them on a plate and set the plate on the coffee table in front of the kids. Eli took one and blew on it and broke it in half and gave half to Gary. Maddie did not take one. Maddie watched Wren.

The first siren came at seven-twenty-six.

She set the phone down on the kitchen island still connected and she went to the front door and unlocked it and opened it and stood on the porch with her hands where they could be seen. Two cruisers. Then a third. Then an ambulance. A young officer came up the walk with his hand near his holster but not on it and she told him, in short sentences, what he needed to hear to let the paramedics past her and into the house.

They took her arm. They took her leg. They asked about the children and she pointed. Maddie was already telling a second officer, in her flat clear voice, about the men and the attic and the babysitter, and the second officer was writing it down and nodding, and at one point Maddie looked across the room at Wren and held her eyes for two seconds and looked back at the officer and said, "I didn't see anything. I was upstairs."

The Mercers arrived at seven-fifty-one. Mrs. Mercer got out of the car screaming her children's names. Mr. Mercer stood on the lawn with his tie loose and his phone at his side and did not move for a long time.

In the noise of it Wren stepped off the back of the ambulance with her arm wrapped and her leg wrapped and she told the paramedic she needed a minute and she walked around the side of the house and through the gap in the hedge she had noticed going in twelve hours ago, and nobody stopped her, because nobody was looking at her yet.

She walked.

Four blocks. Five. The sun was fully up. Her leg was working on borrowed time and she knew it. She sat down on a curb outside a house with a For Sale sign in the yard and put her head between her knees.

There was something in her hand.

She lifted her head and looked.

Gary. The plastic triceratops. She didn't remember taking him. She tried to remember Eli putting him in her hand and couldn't. Somewhere in the couch or the porch or the walk to the ambulance he had pressed the dinosaur into her palm and she had closed her fingers around him without noticing and had carried him out of the house and through the hedge and four blocks down the road.

She sat on the curb with Gary in her lap.

She looked at him for a while.

She did not know what to do with him.

This chapter is a strong piece of pulp fiction writing that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through it carefully.

**Craft and Execution**

The prose is controlled and deliberate. The writer has a clear voice — flat, reportorial, occasionally precise in ways that cut. The opening image of Wren leaving the eight-inch knife on the sideboard because it's "too long for a staircase" is excellent: it establishes competence without glamorizing it, and it's the kind of specific practical detail that earns trust. The smell description — "Sunflower shells and Old Spice aftershave and something sourer underneath, maybe sweat, maybe just old man" — is economical and effective, and it ties directly to the character profile's detail about Cope's sunflower seed habit.

The pacing of the confrontation is well-managed. Cope's dialogue is exactly what the plan called for: no villain monologue, no grand revelation, just a tired man with a small chance at something better. The detail about the tie and Wren's mother is genuinely good — it's specific, it's not sentimental, and it does the work of placing Cope in her history without over-explaining. The exchange "You volunteered." / "Yeah." / "For a promotion." / "That's right." is clean and efficient.

**Character Work**

Cope is rendered faithfully to his profile. The sunflower seeds, the Members Only jacket, the soft body, the patient manner — all present. His eyes going to "disappointment" rather than fear at the end is a strong choice that avoids the cliché of the villain's terrified final moment. It's consistent with a man who bet on a horse and knew the odds were against him.

Wren is also consistent. The plan called for her to feel like she's "finished a chore" afterward, and the prose delivers this without stating it directly. She retties the dishtowel, looks at her leg, notes the forearm bleeding again, notes she has no more towels. The sunflower shells left on the armrest — she leaves them there. That's the right ending beat for the chapter: not poetic, not resonant in a gestured way, just a small fact that carries weight.

**The Fight**

The fight is handled well. The plan called for her to be shot in the thigh and get to him anyway because "the basement is small and she is furious." The execution delivers this: "four steps was nothing, four steps was a held breath" is a good line. The description of the bullet wound — "a bright punched feeling" — is precise without being overwrought. The detail that "adrenaline is a liar that tells useful lies" is one of the chapter's better lines, doing character work and physical description simultaneously.

The plan also called for her to kill him "with her hands and the paring knife and it takes a while." The chapter delivers on the duration and the ugliness without lingering pornographically. The knife through the back of his hand is specific and physical. The hits he lands being "the hits of a man whose hands had mostly held paperwork for ten years" is a good line — it characterizes him while explaining why she survives.

**What Doesn't Quite Land**

The line "She had been a big man's daughter and she knew what a big man felt like under a hand and he did not feel like one" is slightly over-written. It's reaching for resonance in a way that the rest of the chapter mostly avoids. It's not terrible, but it's the chapter's most self-conscious moment.

The plan specified that she "does not feel good afterward. She does not feel bad. She feels like she has finished a chore." The chapter gestures at this but doesn't quite land it as cleanly as the plan describes — the prose registers the aftermath through action (retying the dishtowel, noting the bleeding) rather than any interiority, which is actually the right call, but the plan's specific emotional note is slightly absent. This is a minor criticism; the approach taken is arguably better than stating it.

The chapter plan also mentioned that she kills him "with her hands and the paring knife." The paring knife goes into his hand early, and then the killing is primarily strangulation. This is fine — it's more interesting than a knife kill — but it's a slight departure.

**Dialogue**

The dialogue is one of the chapter's genuine strengths. Cope's voice is exactly right: patient, not cruel, a little sad, not self-pitying. The exchange about the mother is the best dialogue in the chapter. "I'm not claiming I knew her" is a good line. Wren's responses are appropriately minimal. The rhythm of the conversation feels earned.

**Following the Plan**

The chapter follows its plan closely. Cope in the recliner, the gun on the paper towel, the sunflower seeds, the name said out loud, the shot that misses and the shot that hits the thigh, the small basement making the distance closeable. The plan's note about Cope's eyes going to "disappointment" is executed. The plan's note about his hand touching her wrist at the end is executed. The chapter ends where it should — her going to the stairs, not a poetic image.

**Overall Assessment**

This is a well-executed chapter that delivers on its plan without over-reaching. The prose is disciplined. The character work is strong. The violence is physical and unglamorous. The dialogue is the best in the story so far. The chapter avoids the pitfalls the writer identified in the plan — no villain monologue, no stylish kill, no resonant ending image. The one moment of self-consciousness ("She had been a big man's daughter") is a minor flaw in an otherwise controlled piece.
